speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: COLOMBO PLAN-STATEMENT ON ALLOCATION OF CANADIAN FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and the permission of the house I should like, as Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs, to make a short report to the house regarding some recent decisions under our Canadian Colombo plan program in India, Pakistan and Ceylon, and to table a more detailed statement on these matters.
When the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke in the recent external affairs debate he undertook to provide the house with a report on the allocation of Canadian funds to particular projects in the countries to which we are giving assistance as decisions are made on these matters. Since he did not have time before his departure for the NATO conference in Paris to inform the house that approval had been given for Canadian aid to a number of projects in the Colombo plan area and for aid in a variety of forms, and since he will not return in time to do so before the Christmas adjournment, I wish to take this opportunity to do so on his behalf.
The document to be tabled gives in adequate detail a description of all these projects and I propose to do little more orally than to list them. However, I should emphasize that these programs will be financed by funds already voted by parliament or provided for in the main estimates of the Department of External Affairs for the current year, with the one exception of the Indian program. For India these projects, together with the shipment of $7 million worth of wheat, will take up not only the funds now available, but in addition $5 million of the sums which parliament will be asked to vote for the Colombo plan next year. The authority which has now been given for a number of projects and forms of aid will enable purchasing to go forward over the next six to eight months. By making these decisions now subject of course to parliament voting the necessary funds, we are ensuring that Canadian aid will flow as quickly as possible during the next half year.
In this fashion we are endeavouring to speed up the flow of available aid to India.
I should also mention, before listing the projects, that the great bulk of these goods and materials and the engineering services associated with them will be provided from Canadian sources.
With regard to the program in India, Canada proposes to make available a further $2 million to continue work on the Canada-India reactor; $5 million for the erection of transmission lines as part of the Kundah hydroelectric development near Madras; $3 million for treated wooden railway ties; $120,000 for three cobalt beam cancer therapy units; $65,000 for audio-visual equipment and educational material, and $10.8 million for the supply of industrial metals urgently required by India's metal working industry.
With regard to the program in Pakistan, Canada will provide $1 million for the construction of a transmission line for the Ganges-Kobadak project and $1.6 million for the doubling of the circuit on the Dacca-Chittagong electric transmission line.
With regard to our Colombo plan program in Ceylon, hon. members will recall that of the $2 million available for Ceylon $1 million is being supplied in the form of flour which, when sold, will create counterpart funds for use on a number of projects which will be reported to the house in due course. As far as the other $1 million is concerned, Canada will make available a further $200,000 for the construction of additional transmission lines for the river valley development scheme in eastern Ceylon; $12,500 for remedial equipment for the rehabilitation centre at the University of Ceylon; $640,000 for the continuation of the aerial survey; $14,000 for additional agricultural pest control units; $17,500 for a stand-by radio unit for Colombo airport; $3,000 for X-ray maintenance equipment; $100,000 for further equipment for a technical institute, and $13,000 for a crane for Colombo harbour.
With the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, I should like at this time to table the detailed statement with regard to these individual projects.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. Is the minister able to announce at this time any plans to put men to work this winter on outdoor activities which will be of help to the province of British Columbia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilton (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the request of the Minister of Labour the provision of winter employment on projects that could be undertaken by or through the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has been under careful study. The department regularly provides substantial winter work through its operations in the national parks, in northern Canada and in various other fields.
Within the funds that have been made available by parliament, steps have already been taken to carry out additional winter work over and above normal level. Examples of these steps are at Cape Breton Highlands park, Terra Nova park and Prince Edward Island park, where a total of about 200 jobs have already been made available or will be available within a few days.
However, plans have been under way for projects on a much greater scale, providing additional funds are voted by parliament. It is the intention to bring in additional estimates, and if these are voted before January 15 work will be started within a few days thereafter on a series of jobs throughout the national park system, including Wood Buffalo park which is astride the Alberta-Northwest Territories boundary.
These works will include cutting and clearing projects on highways and trails, forest sanitation cutting, preliminary work on camp and picnic ground development, the construction of bungalow camps, and a stepped-up program of building and equipment repair. The work will provide employment from January 15 throughout the winter for some 1,500 persons on the basis of a 44-hour week. Additional work under this same general plan will provide a further 200 jobs on the Mackenzie highway. Between now and January 15 all necessary arrangements will be made so the work can start immediately after that date.
Of these jobs some 600 will be in the western parks, some 400 in the maritimes, and the remainder in the prairie provinces

Inquiries of the Ministry and in the southern part of the Northwest Territories. I will be in close consultation with my colleague the Minister of Labour to ensure that these jobs are filled by persons coming from areas with high rates of unemployment. Most of the work is of an outdoor nature and should, for example, provide substantial assistance in finding jobs for unemployed forest workers in British Columbia. I estimate that this program will provide about
1,000	jobs for the area of the hon. member. I should emphasize that all these projects are of a most useful nature and would have to be undertaken at some time in the next year or two in any event. We are not creating work; we are stepping up our planned program.
I should also mention that further studies are being made at the present time which I am hopeful will result in the provision in the immediate future of an even greater number of jobs than those I have outlined above. As soon as possible I will be glad to make a further announcement as to what we have been able to do.

Inquiries of the Ministry on the Pacific coast. These questions arose out of a letter addressed to me by the united fishermen and allied workers' union.
I may say this is not a new problem. Dogfish, a species of small shark, have been a nuisance to fishermen and a predator on food fish for many years on both the Pacific and Atlantic coasts. In some years there appears to be a greater concentration of these predators than in others.
In 1956 parliament approved a plan to encourage the catching of dogfish on the Pacific coast and their manufacture into meal for animal feed. An amount of $300,000 was voted to give a bounty of $10 per ton on
30,000	tons. Actually only 220 tons of dogfish were caught. The fishermen and the processors could not get together on price and other arrangements.
There is obviously not much point in renewing an offer of this kind. If, however, the fishermen's union along with the operators of the fish reduction plants and the processors of dogfish liver oil would get together and present a jointly agreed proposal which has a reasonable chance of successfully eliminating or reducing the numbers of this predator, the government will be prepared to consider such a proposal carefully.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO AUTHORIZE LOANS FOR ADDITIONAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I would like to make one
or two comments with regard to this bill. In essence the bill is to provide the financing for a project which contemplates substantial and useful enlargements to Hamilton harbour. I think we are all fully impressed with the importance of Hamilton harbour and with the volume of traffic it is now handling.
When we discussed the project on second reading it developed that the total cost is likely to be about $8 million, of which $4 million is to be advanced by the government under this bill as a loan to the Hamilton harbour commissioners, and the other $4 million is to be provided by the Department of Public Works. I take it that in due course we shall have the opportunity of dealing with the estimates which will be brought forward for that purpose, but I would like to draw to the attention of the minister particularly that this is quite a significant departure from past practices in the sense that I think, broadly speaking, it has not been the practice of previous governments to defray even in part the expenditures which are made by these autonomous harbour commissioners. It might therefore create a precedent which other harbour commissioners will expect to have followed in their own cases.
For example, in the case of some of the harbours coming under the national harbours board the full cost of those improvements is, in effect, assessed against the local harbour in the accounts of the national harbours board. If one builds a large wharf for Montreal, for example, at a cost of $4 million, that $4 million forms part of the investment of the national harbours board in the Montreal harbour and no part is paid by the taxpayers at large. It forms part of the accounts of the national harbours board, and the interest and amortization of the cost is taken care of through the revenues from that particular harbour in the accounts of the board.
Hamilton Harbour Commissioners
In this particular case what is really happening is that approximately half the cost will be furnished, interest free, by the federal government to this harbour commission. During the course of the discussion of the bill in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines this subject was touched on very briefly; to this extent, that I asked Mr. Harstone, who was the chairman of the commission, what would be the additional revenues which would accrue to the commission from the construction of the proposed facilities. He said in round figures they had estimated it would be approximately $230,000. That was the additional revenue that would be received from the three projects which would be financed under this bill.
That seems to suggest rather clearly that the harbour would not be capable of bearing the interest cost of the whole investment of $8 million, because even if one calculates principal and interest at an annual rate of 5 per cent on $8 million, one sees that the annual charge would be at least $400,000, and consequently the revenues which would be available to the commission from these projects, at least, would not be sufficient to make them self-sustaining.
But I would like to say to the minister that I realize that is not the issue in this bill. The issue in the bill is whether or not $4 million is to be loaned to the commission, and there is no doubt from the evidence placed before the committee that the commission would be able to service the principal and interest on this $4 million.
I fully expect that when the Minister of Public Works brings before the house his estimates with regard to the balance of the cost, he will then be in a position to supply us with a more detailed statement of the economics of the situation than we had in the committee, and I am sure hon. members will appreciate that we were under some disability in that connection in that we could hardly make that an issue in the discussion of a loan project.
However, when it comes to voting the government contribution to this project I fully expect the Minister of Public Works, who is always most anxious to provide the fullest information on everything under the sun, will bring with him information as to the economics of this particular project so we may see how fully it has been justifiable to depart from the ordinary process, or perhaps I should say the ordinary procedure, of allowing the autonomous harbour commissioners to finance their own improvements.

We have an economic studies branch of the Department of Public Works, and before any legislation was brought forward they had made a very careful study of this whole Hamilton harbour situation in co-operation with the officials from the Department of Transport. As a result of that study it was found that the payment of charges on one-half the investment required for these works in Hamilton harbour would be about as much as the commissioners could undertake at this time.
Here is the basis for government policy as represented by this bill. There is no such thing as a uniform policy in all the harbour commissions. Each harbour must be dealt with on the merits of that particular harbour. There are, as the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount knows, several other harbour commissions, and the Department of Public Works has built almost all the public facilities in Winnipeg-St. Boniface, Port Al-berni, North Fraser, Belleville-

There will be developments in other harbours as a result of the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway which will have to be paid for at least in part by the Department of Public Works. Take for example Fort William-Port Arthur. I wrote a letter to the mayors of these two cities just a few days

ago outlining the results of the surveys made, again by the economic studies branch of the Departments of Public Works and Transport. We have also investigated Sault Ste. Marie and the need for harbour developments there as a result of the opening of the seaway. That report is not yet available. Today our investigation team is down in the city of Windsor investigating the need for developments at Windsor.
These activities are all being carried out with great dispatch in an attempt to meet the needs in these different centres, and I suggest to the hon. member that this proposal that the Department of Public Works should pay half the cost and the harbour commissions pay the other half is a very reasonable plan.
As a matter of fact, before this policy was adopted the Department of Public Works had been paying everything. Now the department is only having to find one half, so to adopt the policy urged by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount and make the harbour commission pay all the cost would be very detrimental to the city of Hamilton and to the area served by that great city.
The hon. member made some statements on December 3 about this question which were not accurate. For example, he said:

speechtext: What other purpose could the bill have?

speechtext:
I am not suggesting that it has. I am simply pointing out that is the only purpose it does have. I am pointing that out because it is on that premise I want to found the rest of what I have to say about this measure.
It is rather surprising, as the hon. member for Laurier pointed out last evening, that at a conference which was called for the purpose of discussing general fiscal relations between the federal and provincial governments, at a conference about which before it was held it was very difficult for those of us on this side of the house to find out whether any other subjects could be discussed at all, that the only kind of concrete proposal put forward by the federal government was a proposal to do something about a measure that, so far as I have been able to discover, no provincial government has made any specific request in public to have anything done about.
I find it very difficult to reconcile this course of action on the part of the federal government with the so-called new attitude toward the provinces about which the Prime Minister spoke at the opening of the federal-provincial conference on November 25. I am quoting from the official record of the conference and from the Prime Minister's opening observations which, as one would expect in the circumstances, were televised. This is what the Prime Minister said:
In welcoming you, too, I would point out that you will have noted by this time there is some change in the faces of the occupants of the portfolios of the government of Canada that has taken place in recent months, and I hope, too, that we shall also show a change in philosophy and in outlook to some of the problems facing our country.
It has been said, Mr. Chairman, by the Prime Minister, by other members of the government and by their supporters in this house that the present government had made a great change from the previous government in its attitude toward the provincial governments. It has been charged over and over again that we adopted a take it or leave it attitude and that the present government was going to change all that, that it was going to listen to the provinces; and the implication was that it was going to do what the provinces wanted it to do.
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, I do not think that was a proper description of the attitude of the preceding government. I call to witness-and I think I should put this on the record-one whom I think it would be extremely hard for hon. gentlemen opposite to disavow. I propose to put on the record what Mr. Frost, the premier of Ontario, said

about previous conferences under the previous government and the way in which they were conducted. What he said does not support or bear out in any way the kind of criticism that has been made of the attitude of the previous government toward the provincial governments. Mr. Frost was speaking about the present Leader of the Opposition, my right hon. friend the hon. member for Quebec East, and he said:
Now at this moment in history, because it is a moment of history, when he is no longer chairman of this conference and when he is retiring from his leadership of his party, I would like to express my admiration for him which has been well known and which I have stated here on many other occasions. Of course, like the prime minister of Quebec-
I say "premier".
-I have disagreed with him in regard to matters of policy but I have never disagreed with him as a personality and as a great Canadian.
This is Mr. Frost whom I am quoting.
As I say I would like today to again express my appreciation for his ability as chairman over several conferences and meetings and my thanks for his infinite patience which he has invariably shown, for his unfailing courtesy which I think sprang from Mr. St. Laurent himself and from the fact that he was, centrally, a Canadian gentleman and came from that great race one of the attributes of which is courtesy and understanding.
I think it is useful to have on the record this opinion from one who has never been a supporter of my right hon. friend, about the way in which our government conducted its relations with the provinces. To those of us who attended, as I did, at all but a few minutes of the open sessions of the federal-provincial	conference-and I make no
apology for referring to it as the federal-provincial conference-in November, it was perfectly clear that all the premiers there really came desiring-and that was what they said publicly-to have the central issue discussed; and the central issue, of course, was the apportionment between the federal government and the provincial governments of the tax revenues from the three principal direct taxes which have been the subject of these various discussions between the federal and provincial governments ever since 1945.
When they got there they found that the federal government had no proposals to make, had not even any suggestions to make, had not even any hints as to how this fiscal matter would be dealt with, and that despite repeated attempts by the premiers of Manitoba and Saskatchewan to get from the federal government an admission that the principle of equalization would continue to be applied in any additional apportionment of these taxes, no such commitment could be secured from the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance.

I know the hon. gentlemen opposite prefer to announce their policies elsewhere than in this house, but until such policies are announced in this house it is very hard for us in our deliberations to take them very seriously.
The federal-provincial conference, as I shall continue to call it, was convoked for the purpose of discussing general fiscal relations between the federal and provincial governments; at least that is what the premiers were told. The country expected many serious things to come of this conference, but instead at the opening we had the Prime Minister making this statement about the matter which is now before the committee, and I shall quote from the official record of the conference for Monday, November 25, at page C-3:
That brings me to a question that has been discussed on a number of occasions-the request of some provinces for the removal of the so-called "threshold" of .45 per cent under the Unemployment Assistance Act. Its removal would have the result that the dominion treasury would share the costs of all eligible cases upon the relief rolls- whether employable or unemployable-and not just the numbers in excess of .45 per cent of the provincial population. We should then be avoiding entirely this invidious distinction between employable and unemployable persons and sharing the costs of providing aid to all those in need, apart from the normal statutory responsibilities of the provinces in respect of mothers' allowances.
I am told that a change of this nature would make it much easier for some suitable arrangements to be made to assist their municipalities which have been carrying most of this burden of assistance to those in need, apart of course from the bulk of the cost being carried by unemployment insurance. The benefits of removing this "threshold" would be fairly equitably divided among all the provinces that would be participating in agreements under this act, and we see no serious obstacle to meeting your wishes in this regard.
I find this a very very puzzling statement. As I say, there is nothing I have been able to find in the records anywhere to suggest that any provincial governments were seriously concerned about the removal of this threshold, and I think I might perhaps remind you, sir, and the members of this committee that this threshold was there precisely to avoid the invidious distinction to which the Prime Minister refers, between the employable and unemployable person.

Unemployment Assistance Act
For no other reason was it put there. It was put there on the assumption, and a quite sensible assumption it was too, that the .45 per cent of the provincial population represented an average of the cases of public charity and assistance to the normally unemployable who have always been regarded, ever since confederation, as a provincial responsibility. The federal government has never taken any responsibility for that group, and it was in order to preserve that constitutional distinction without creating any hardship to individuals that my right hon. friend devised, recommended and persuaded this parliament to enact the present legislation.
I therefore suggest, sir, that my hon. friend the member for Laurier was perfectly right last night when he said that in removing this threshold all the government is doing is making an invasion of provincial rights and taking a very big step toward centralization, against which they have preached-I was going to say so hypocritically, but I suppose that would be unparliamentary-

Well, I should like to get on with my speech. I think that would be more productive than any exchange with the hon. member for Carleton, amusing though it might be for him.
I want to say one or two things about what was said last night by the hon. member for Nanaimo, because he did deal with a very serious problem and one which all of us in this house are going to have to face as a result of the increasing unemployment we are bound to have during the next few months; that is, the whole question of responsibility for unemployment assistance. In saying something about this I should like to correct the impression-not to correct the facts, because I think the hon. gentleman's facts were perfectly correct

but to correct the impression he gave in the course of the recital of certain facts last evening.
The first thing the hon. gentleman said to which I take some exception was that in 1937, at the time the Rowell-Sirois commission was appointed, the provinces enjoyed revenues from personal income and corporation taxes. That seemed to imply that they do not have them now. That is not true at all. The fact is that the revenue which the provinces derive from these tax fields is manifestly greater today than it was in 1937, and a very large part of this revenue comes in the form of equalization payments, the purpose of which is to put the provinces and the provincial treasuries in a position to discharge their responsibility for themselves; and it seems to me that this principle of equalization which has been imported into our federal-provincial relations since 1945 does change the whole picture in respect to this matter.
I am not saying for one moment that this necessarily means there may not be situations arise in which parliament should assume full responsibility for unemployment assistance. I do not think, however, that any government with any sense of responsibility would undertake the financial burden of unemployment assistance in full unless it also undertook the administration. I should be very surprised if any government, even a government as reckless as the one we have at the present time, would undertake such a
Unemployment Assistance Act course of action. That, of course, would involve a very much greater degree of centralization than we in this party have been willing to embark upon.
I consider that though this measure will certainly be welcomed, I imagine, by every provincial treasurer whose government has made an agreement with the federal government, it would have been much more welcome to most of them if the government had gone ahead with what it promised to do before the election and produced the new fiscal deal which it promised.

speechtext: If it had done so the provinces would already be in a position to do something on their own, not merely to pay unemployment assistance but also to get on with a good many useful and badly needed works-and I can certainly speak about the province of Newfoundland-which would have the effect of diminishing the amount of unemployment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REMOVE THRESHOLD PROVISION FROM AGREEMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have to go back some considerable time in our history before we reach a period similar to that through which our country is passing today. I think my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo yesterday gave a very clear illustration of the situation when Canada was faced with problems similar to those which confront us now. He made reference to the setting up of the Rowell-Sirois commission which dealt particularly with this question of unemployment, the subject matter of the present bill. As I understand the report of that commission, it was suggested that responsibility for the unemployed of this country should be divided in the following manner, namely that the provinces should accept full responsibility for the unemployable-people physically unable to work- while the federal government should accept responsibility for unemployed employables.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder what is the use of going to the expense of setting up these royal commissions to devote great care to the study of these questions when the recommendations which are finally made are not acted upon. Two or three royal commissions have been set up this session by this government to consider various problems. If the recommendations of these commissions are not going to be acted upon any more than the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois commission, it would seem to me a waste of time and money to keep them sitting.
Let us consider this question of responsibility and the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois commission. The whole matter puts me in mind of the old story of the

Unemployment Assistance Act constitution of horse and rabbit stew in the armed forces canteen. Under this recipe one horse equalled one rabbit. Under the terms of the commission's recommendation the rabbit would be the responsibility of the province-the relatively small number unable to work. The horse-in this case a situation such as we are fast approaching, namely a terrific number of unemployed people-would be the responsibility of the federal government. But now, instead of each accepting his share, we find that the federal government is proposing to share the cost. In other words they will pay for half the rabbit, but they want the province to look after half their horse.
Moreover, I see that the division of responsibility in the old days of the depression was supposed to be on a 40-40-20 basis, the 20 per cent being paid by the municipalities, and I also note that under this new offer from the federal government to raise its proportion by 10 per cent, my own province of Ontario has decreased its contribution from 40 to 30 per cent.
That is the proposition. In other words it is a straight transfer of 10 per cent from the Ontario government to the federal government. That certainly is not going to aid the municipalities. I think we have had it amply demonstrated to us in the past that the municipalities are completely and physically unable to cope with the situation of unemployment. The municipal governments do not have the sources of revenue in their taxation fields which would allow them to meet this situation in any way, shape or form.
Further than that, there is very little the municipalities can do to change the policies or lack of policies that cause these periods of unemployment from time to time. I believe that responsibility rests with the federal government, and in cases like this it should accept that responsibility. If it cannot ensure that we will not have these blights of unemployment every so often in our country, at least it should do something to lift the load from the provincial governments and certainly from the municipal governments.
I have here the latest figures for unemployment I could find, prepared as of November 14, 1957. This table gives the unemployment picture for Canada as a whole and breaks it down by provinces and even by regions. I have not found this too satisfactory, at least on the local basis. I do not know just in what region my constituency would fall according to the regional breakdown in this table. The closest area I can see geographically is the region of Sudbury, which is stated to have 2,736 unemployed at the present time.

As president of the Timmins Cochrane and district labour council I have had occasion to see just what the situation is in my locality. Local 2995 of the lumber and sawmill workers union is the bargaining agent for the bush workers, log cutters and other similar workers in the northern area. Normally at this time it has between 7,000 and 8,000 dues paying members in the local. Last week the figure was down to 1,200, I believe. I don't know where the balance of these people totalling approximately 6,000 are listed on this table. Perhaps they are listed in some other locality according to this breakdown; either that or my region is not listed at all.
Certainly those 6,000 people in that area will be absolutely beyond the means of the municipality to help. I think the story is pretty much the same across the country. The municipal governments are in desperate straits trying to meet the present calls on their resources, and certainly are unable to meet any new situations such as the one confronting us at the present time.
There is another point I would like to raise at this time. The figures to which I referred represent a list of the unemployed in Canada. I presume it shows merely the total number of people who are unemployed, those who might be described as wage earners. I wonder if this table takes into account the members of their families. Do these figures account for just the head of the family, the wage earner? If we also take into consideration the number of dependants of each of these unemployed, then on the basis of these figures there would be in the neighbourhood of one and a half million who can expect to experience a pretty bleak Christmas this year.
We have seen at lot of activity in the country to the south of us and more recently in this country on the part of certain groups who are aggressively advocating what they term as right to work laws. Anyone familiar with the trade union movement realizes full well that these are not right to work laws at all. Rather they are the right to go through picket lines, the right to refuse to participate in union shops and closed shops; in other words the right to try to undermine all the union security that presently exists in this country. I believe in right to work laws, but I believe these words should be taken for just what they say. I believe that each of these 352,000 unemployed people- and I understand this figure has increased tremendously in the past month because, as I said, these are the figures for November, 1957-has a right to work.
Even if this bill is improved beyond its present terms it certainly is not going to be

a solution to the unemployment problem. There is only one solution to unemployment and that is employment. I maintain that if half the effort, time and ingenuity that in the past have gone into this buck passing among the federal, provincial and municipal governments in trying to decide who is responsible for these unemployed people had been put into making jobs available for them, we certainly would not be faced with the unemployment problem that confronts us today.
I do not know how many hon. members have been in the position of some of these unemployed. I do not know if they realize just how demoralizing it can be to a man who is willing and able to work but who cannot find a job, when he sees his wife and family depending on him and through no fault of his own he is unable to provide a living for them. It is certainly an extremely demoralizing experience. There can be no doubt but that he would tend to lose faith not only in our way of life and the system under which we operate, but would also become highly fertile ground for the spread of the dread disease of communism. I believe it is in fields like this that communists can spread their propaganda in the world today.
In drawing my remarks to a close I would like to add one point. If this government feels it is helpless to meet this emergency any better than it has been met in the past with all the resources at its disposal in this nation, then how in the world can the government expect the municipalities and provinces and in the final analysis the wage earning head of the family with the limited resources at his disposal-his only resource being his ability to work, which is denied him when he is unemployed-to meet the situation?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not expected to take up the time of the committee in an attempt to hold up this measure because I think it is most desirable, but the unemployment situation in my constituency is such that I should like to call upon the government to give whatever assistance is possible. When I picked up my morning paper, the Windsor Daily Star, I noted that as of December 5, 1957, there were 14,052 people unemployed. I trust that the word "unemployed" is not unparliamentary. In some circles it is felt that it is a word which should not be used, but being an old-fashioned person I think we should describe a situation by the word that conveys the proper connotation and meaning.
As I said, there were 14,052 persons unemployed as of December 5. These for the most part are middle class people, hard working, conscientious, honest and industrious. They are just the average type of citizen one
Unemployment Assistance Act finds throughout the length and breadth of this country. Many of them are expert mechanics or craftsmen who were employed in the automobile factories and its feeder plants in the city. These people are not anxious to be in this situation; they are people who deplore the situation and are most anxious to help themselves as much as possible.
For that reason they are looking for assistance to provide an atmosphere wherein industry may thrive and business may be carried on successfully and profitably. They are asking for an atmosphere where there is some measure of security and assurance. We have many projects through which work could be provided. It is not to their liking to be accepting unemployment insurance, although it is theirs as of right; it is insurance they have bought and paid for. But it is not the natural state of man to be unemployed and inactive. For that reason these people are most anxious to be working, to be doing things and taking part in production and the building up of the country.
There are many projects which could be used properly by the government to advance the welfare of the country as a whole. I suggest the construction of highways. In my constituency we would also like to have a post office built at one place, and it has been in the planning stage for a considerable time. I note that recently the Minister of Public Works decided he would proceed with the project. Ever since the opening day of the session I have been pressing him to get along with it. Apparently it could not be done until just recently, but I understand he has now decided he can proceed with the work expeditiously. For this I congratulate him, and I hope he will make good his promise and see that the construction of this building is proceeded with promptly.
There are many other projects of a semi if not wholly national aspect. A sewage disposal plant is needed for sewage going into international waters. The municipality cannot hope to complete it because it involves an expenditure of at least $25 million to $30 million. If it is not proceeded with considerable hardship will be created for the people in that community. We are also building an auditorium and we would like some assistance there if it could be arranged. I realize that the building of an auditorium is not necessarily a national project, but there are precedents in regard to other projects throughout the country which are not of a national character.
I refer particularly to the policy of the government announced yesterday by the Minister of Justice, whereby assistance is

Unemployment Assistance Act to be given to the people of a particular mining community and the sum of $16,000 a month is to be expended from the federal treasury to help maintain them. Therefore I make a particular plea on behalf of the
14,000	people in my constituency who are unemployed at the present time. That number may be increased very shortly because of declining conditions, and I urge the government to follow the precedent they have set by providing assistance through work and the promotion and development of the assets of this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REMOVE THRESHOLD PROVISION FROM AGREEMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this legislation will provide some additional funds for some of the provincial treasuries of the country and will be of at least a little assistance with regard to the unemployment situation. Therefore we shall support the legislation. I confess, however, that we do not intend to wax very eloquent about it, because no one can claim that it is a major piece of legislation.
I have taken the trouble to read through the debate on unemployment that took place in the house starting on March 2, 1955, on an amendment to the motion to go into supply moved by the present Secretary of State. I have also read the debate that took place in 1956 when the Unemployment Assistance Act was put on the statute books, and the things the Tories called for in those two debates by way of an attack on the problem of unemployment were a lot more than is suggested by the measure now being presented to the house.
I also want to agree with one or two things the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said. I will make it clear shortly that I disagree with some of his comments. I agree with him that this measure is a poor substitute for the improvement in federal provincial fiscal arrangements that we were led to believe would be undertaken early in the regime of the new Prime Minister. Some hon. members opposite complained when the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate raised this question, but the fact is that we were led to believe that something would be done with regard to federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, and so far only two or three little things like this have reached the light of day. We have to accept them as the moves the government is making in that direction, but this little move is a very poor substitute for real improvement in federal-provincial fiscal arrangements.
It is also a poor substitute for an assurance from the government that the principle of equalization will be maintained in those arrangements. I come from one of two provinces, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, where

the governments and the people are deeply concerned lest the direction in which federal-provincial fiscal arrangements seem to be going may mean the losing of that equalization principle to the detriment of the economic position of those two provinces. I confess that that is a larger subject of which this is only a small part, but on behalf of the people of those two provinces, indeed on behalf of the people of Canada as a whole, on behalf of national unity, I urge that the equalization principle be maintained in federal-provincial fiscal arrangements.
This measure is not only a poor substitute for a larger measure of improvement in federal-provincial fiscal arrangements; it is also a poor substitute for what has been talked about for many years with regard to federal responsibility for the employable unemployed. When I say this has been talked about for many years, I want to make it clear it has been advocated in years gone by both by Liberals and by Conservatives. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate suggested that certain changes had taken place in the meantime, and I will come to those in a few moments.
First of all may I remind him, and Liberals generally, that the position of the Liberals for many years was that the responsibility for the employable unemployed should rest with the federal government. In that connection I was rather amazed last night to hear the hon. member for Laurier say this, as recorded at page 2572 of Hansard for December 18, 1957:
Since the federal-provincial conferences of 1945 and 1946 it has been customary to make a distinction between employable and unemployable unemployed, and in recent years the federal government has offered to participate with the provinces in the cost of assistance to employable unemployed not receiving unemployment insurance benefits.
I emphasize that the hon. member said that the former government, during recent years, had been offering to participate with the provinces in these costs. May I remind him, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and other Liberals that in line with the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois commission the former Liberal government, at the federal-provincial conference of 1945, made it clear that it believed not just in participating with the provinces but in full federal responsibility for the employable unemployed.
I hold in my hand a copy of one of the green books prepared in connection with that conference. It is the one entitled "Proposals of the Government of Canada", and starting

on page 42 there is a section under the heading "Unemployment Assistance". I read one or two sentences:
The dominion government in its statement on employment and income, announced that the maintenance of a high level of employment and income was "a primary object of policy".
In other words the federal government admitted responsibility for something we claim is a federal responsibility, that is the level of employment itself. One of the reasons that the federal government, in our view, must not try to pass the responsibility for the maintenance of employable unemployed to the provinces is because it is primarily a federal responsibility as to whether or not our economic situation will be such that there will be a high level of employment. I submit that was implied in the position taken at the 1945 federal-provincial conference by the then federal government, and it is implied in the sentence I have just read.
I go farther down on the same page and there are these words:
The dominion is therefore accompanying its proposal for general acceptance of responsibility-
That is responsibility for the employable unemployed.
-with a concrete plan for its Implementation in the field of assistance for employable unemployed persons.
Over on page 43, amongst other details that are spelled out, there is this paragraph:
(d) The plan proposes acceptance of dominion responsibility for unemployed employables and provincial and local responsibility for unemployables, but it is recognized that this division presents problems of definition in some individual cases, and that in operating practice the only final test of employability is ability to get and hold a job.
It is quite true that later in the story the former prime minister sought to deal with the problem as to how you draw the line between employable and unemployable by this .45 per cent formula, but even the devising of that formula did not detract from the position taken by the Liberals in 1945 that the responsibility for the employable unemployed rests with the federal government.

speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? I am quite sure he wants to be completely fair about this. Is it not true that this offer to assume responsibility for assistance to the employable unemployed was part of a package deal, and was never offered in any other way? This was turned down by certain of the provinces, and as a result the tax rental payments, as they were then called, were substantially increased because it had not been possible to get agreement.
Unemployment Assistance Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REMOVE THRESHOLD PROVISION FROM AGREEMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is
correct that the proposals made in 1945 were part of a package deal, and because that conference blew up we did not get the package. Across the years we have managed to get out of this and former governments some of the elements that were in that package such as improvements in old age pensions; the beginning of a health grants program; the beginning of a hospital insurance program, and so on.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate says we have a different situation in that we now have equalization payments. I submit that that is essentially a part of the financial aspect of the package of 1945, and that the change the hon. member says has taken place does not change the basic fact which the Liberals accepted in 1945, namely that the central government is the government that is mainly responsible for those policies that determine the level of economic activity in the country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REMOVE THRESHOLD PROVISION FROM AGREEMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: We never denied that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO REMOVE THRESHOLD PROVISION FROM AGREEMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
am glad to hear the hon. member's statement. I take it he will agree with me that it is still the case, and that being the case we contend that if the central government, which is primarily responsible for economic policies, tries to push responsibility for the maintenance of the employable unemployed on to the provinces it is shirking something which is the responsibility of the central government. If the federal government is going to get out from under, either the former government or the new government, the consequences of policies that create unemployment, it is not going to be under the same impetus to maintain policies that will provide full employment as it would if it were faced with its full responsibilities in that field.
Along with these equalization payments which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and I hope will be continued, there have come increased responsibilities so far as the provinces are concerned in all the fields of social security and social welfare. I submit that none of the changes to which the hon. member referred alter the basic picture that was so well set out in the green book proposals of 1945, which were based on the studies of the Rowell-Sirois commission a few years earlier. It is our view, therefore, that the country is being let down in connection with the proposal for 100 per cent federal responsibility for employable unemployed, because that was not implemented by the government that went out of office on June 21 and it is not being implemented by the government that is now in power.

Unemployment Assistance Act
It has been a matter of interest to me in reading the green book proposals and the debates that took place in 1945, as well as in reading the debate on unemployment insurance in 1940, to notice the way in which the view was expressed that we should deal with this matter before the situation became serious. We are heading into a situation that is very serious right now, with unemployment just about 5 per cent of the working force. That was the picture in the middle of November, and it is probably over 5 per cent of the working force now.
We think it is a sorry picture with whatever government is in power, Liberal or Conservative, that this principle of 100 per cent federal responsibility for the employable unemployed seems to be forgotten.
I suggest that the Liberals have put themselves in a rather strange position in this debate yesterday and today. First of all there is this contrast between the readiness to assume 100 per cent of this responsibility back in 1945 and the position taken by the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in this debate, that the 50 per cent share is adequate under what they refer to as the changed conditions.
I think it is also very interesting to notice the difference in the points of view expressed by the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate I think in the very first paragraph of his speech said that he would be voting for the bill. The hon. member for Laurier last night characterized the bill as an invasion of a provincial right. He pointed out that to his amazement even Mr. Duplessis was supporting this invasion, this move in the direction of centralization. In other words, after I listened to what the hon. member for Laurier said last night and after I read again this morning the record of what he said, it seemed to me to be fairly clear that he has no alternative but to vote against the measure. He says it is centralization.

have read with interest the debate on the Unemployment Assistance Act when it was put on the statute books in 1956. The chief spokesman for the Progressive Conservatives, who were then in opposition, was the hon. lady who is now the Secretary of State. Let me give one or two quotations from the hon. lady just in order to show the tone of that debate. On June 28, 1956, as recorded at page 5573 of Hansard of that date, she said:
No, Mr. Chairman. We were very happy to cooperate with the minister last evening and again today in trying to get this bill through the house for the reasons which he explained to us. But I would think if the minister wants to get this bill through the house, he jolly well had better quit . making political speeches.
The minister to whom she was referring there, of course, was the hon. member for Essex East. Then at another point the hon. lady said:
I tell the minister to cut out this nonsense. I tell him either to lay no claim to these false virtues or else put in the act something which will actually give the provinces the thing which he claims he is giving here and which he is not giving.
Those two quotations represent faithfully the character of the debate that took place on that occasion, during which the present Secretary of State and others complained that the Liberals who were then in power had

scuttled their 1945 green book proposals. The hon. member tor Hamilton West complained that this measure, this Unemployment Assistance Act, was not providing for federal responsibility to the extent of 100 per cent for the employable unemployed, and she quoted from the green book proposals of 1945 and condemned the Liberals out of hand for having put those proposals on the shelf. She complained also that even this 50 per cent of assistance that the federal government was prepared to give for those over the .45 per cent threshold was not all it was cracked up to be because administration costs, health and hospital costs and that sort of thing were still left either to the provinces or the municipalities.
Hence the whole story of that debate in 1956, so far as the case made by the Conservatives was concerned, was that this measure did not go far enough. Their whole point was that the Liberals should still come through with their 1945 promise for 100 per cent federal responsibility for the employable unemployed. The hon. lady and her colleagues are now on the government side of the house. They can carry out the Liberals' promises which they condemned the Liberals for not carrying out. But are they doing so? No; they are bringing in a bill which the hon. member for Timmins has characterized so well by his reference to the horse and the rabbit. They are bringing in a bill which makes no change in the percentage that Ottawa puts up so far as the employable unemployed are concerned. All they give by way of an improvement is the offer that the federal government will pay 50 per cent of the relief costs of the unemployable unemployed, those who are now excluded by that threshold formula. It seems to me that if the Liberals look strange in the stand they are taking on this bill, the Conservatives look equally strange.
We think the Rowell-Sirois commission, to which a distinguished member of this house rendered great service during the days when that commission met, and those who prepared the green book proposals of 1945 laid before the country some very sensible, tangible and constructive policies so far as unemployment is concerned. We still think those proposals should be carried out and that this government should not ask us to get enthusiastic about this bill which merely removes that threshold but which still leaves, to use the words of the Secretary of State, the provinces and the municipalities having to carry not just 50 per cent of the load so far as the employable unemployed are concerned but more than 50 per cent, because of their responsibility for administration costs, for health and hospital costs and so on.
Unemployment Assistance Act
I indicated a moment ago that I had done some reading of bygone debates with reference to this matter. One of the debates that interested me a great deal was the debate in 1940 when the Unemployment Insurance Act was first put upon the statute books. Many of those who took part in that debate are no longer with us, but one hon. gentleman is. I refer to the hon. member for Essex East. He welcomed the introduction by the government of which he was a supporter of the unemployment insurance scheme, but he wanted it to be made crystal clear that unemployment insurance by itself was not enough, was not all that the federal government should be doing. On July 19, 1940, as recorded at page 1777 of Hansard, the then hon. member for Essex East, who again is just the hon. member for Essex East, had this to say:
No unemployment insurance scheme in any part of the world has yet been able to operate without calling from time to time upon the national exchequer for further assistance, and for us to assume today that there will in the course of time be no further demands upon the treasury is, I think, not to face realities.
Then over on page 1778 he continued that theme by saying:
This legislation, as far as I can see, does not envisage all the possibilities, and it falls short of adequate consideration of what the perfected legislation in England has taken into consideration, namely, that during a period of prolonged depression, or during a period such as the present when the depression is certainly less acute, unemployment insurance in itself is not sufficient to meet the needs presented by a situation of that sort and must be related to the question of unemployment relief, to the question of the rehabilitation of labour, and to such questions as national health insurance and the like. All these matters are part of a composite scheme-
Another package I might say to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
-and consequently when the hon. gentleman said that he agreed with my interjection as to the impossibility of unemployment insurance ever doing away with relief, he concurs, I take it, in the view that unemployment insurance and unemployment assistance or unemployment relief must go hand in hand.
There was a recognition in this by the hon. member for Essex East way back in 1940 that if the federal government is going to concern itself with unemployment it cannot stop just with unemployment insurance; it has to concern itself with unemployment assistance as well and with all these other matters that are part of a composite scheme.
I would suggest Mr. Chairman, that this is of a piece with the position that the Liberals took back in 1945 and which the Conservatives tried to get the Liberals to take in 1956, that responsibility for employable unemployed should rest with the federal government.

Unemployment Assistance Act Now to come back to the point I made in answer to my hon. friend from Newfoundland a little while ago, that the basic fact about all this-and he agrees with me-is that it is the central government that is primarily responsible for the economic policies in this country and it is the central government whose policies determine whether we will have a high or a low level of employment, we contend very strongly that that being the case, the central government should be responsible for the consequences of those policies. You do not carry out that responsibility by passing 50 per cent of the cost of looking after the employable unemployed to the provinces. We contend therefore that the Rowell-Sirois commission was right; we contend that the Liberals were right in their green book proposals; we contend that the hon. member for Essex East was right when he was speaking on unemployment insurance in 1940; we contend that the Secretary of State was right when, in 1956, she called on the Liberal government to stand by this principle which had been laid down across the years, that the responsibility for employable unemployed should rest 100 per cent with the federal government.

federal minister on several points remaining at issue between us, and only yesterday, on our arrival in Ottawa, received notification from the Minister of National Health and Welfare that these representations had been rejected, and indicating quite clearly that redress could be secured only by carrying our case to the Exchequer Court.
The agreement is unnecessarily complicated and expensive to administer. The complicated assistance formula, with its inclusions and exclusions, its formula of .45 per cent of population, its use of annual population estimates, and its references to mothers' allowance cases whose costs are in no way shared by Canada, has produced administrative problems of the most difficult order, and a need for completely new administrative machinery -the cost of which must be borne entirely by the province and the municipalities.
Moreover, we believe that the agreement is discriminatory as between provinces. It allows certain cases to be included in the claims of one province and excludes exactly the same type of case from the claims of another province, simply because of variations existing in their legislative provisions at the time the agreement was signed.
For example, families of dependent disabled men may be included in the claims of some provinces because these cases are municipal relief responsibilities in those provinces. The same kinds of cases may not, however, be included in Manitoba's claims because they are receiving payments from our provincial mothers' allowance appropriation.
Manitoba is anxiously awaiting lor some solution to these problems. We are hoping that these objections will be met. As a matter of fact, we are under the impression that the present Minister of National Health and Welfare is the type who will not adopt a take it or leave it attitude.

While we are discussing the resolution on unemployment assistance I think we should not forget the Unemployment Insurance Act which, of course, is an act of parliament designed to meet at least part of the problem of those who find themselves without work. As I understand it, when the present Unemployment Insurance Act was first introduced it was as the result of an amendment to the British North America Act which added the words "unemployment insurance".
I suppose that technically one could argue that the inclusion of the words "unemployment insurance" as part of the federal jurisdiction and responsibility under the British North America Act does not of itself put the question of unemployment completely within federal jurisdiction. But I think the people of Canada quite rightly can infer that when that amendment was made to the British North America Act it was made with the idea that we were going to have a system of unemployment insurance under federal jurisdiction which would meet the problem of providing at least some income to those who become unemployed.
It has become obvious, to me at least, as the discussion has progressed that these two questions of the Unemployment Assistance Act, which comes under the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Unemployment Insurance Act, which comes under the Minister of Labour, are difficult to separate in our thinking when dealing with the unemployment situation. As a matter of fact, I do not know whether or not the Minister of National Health and Welfare was intending to indicate how closely these matters are related in his mind, but I did notice that according to yesterday's Hansard, when he was introducing this resolution, inadvertently or otherwise, the minister referred to the Unemployment Insurance Act instead of the Unemployment Assistance Act.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Has that not been corrected?

Not in the copy of Hansard I have in my hand. I assume the minister did that inadvertently or that it was a misunderstanding on the part of the Hansard reporter. Perhaps this lends some weight to the argument my colleagues have been advancing that instead of talking about the removal of this threshold we more properly perhaps should be considering the changing of that 50 per cent contribution-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair. I said I was going to vote for this measure as is.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is exactly what I was going to say next. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said he was going to vote for this measure as it is, and he gave the reason that it would put some dollars into the treasury of his adopted province.
That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
How
many dollars would it put into that treasury? According to the figures of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, $130,000 a year. If instead of removing the threshold, the present government or the former had gone in for 100 per cent of the cost of assistance to the employable unemployed above the threshold it would have put into the treasury of Newfoundland $1,562,058.32 a year. That indicates the difference in terms of provinces that are hit by unemployment between the one approach and the other. The contrast is not so sharp in the case of my own province. But again, Manitoba would do better under

100 per cent above the threshold rather than 50 per cent below the threshold. In the case of Manitoba, under the changes proposed in this legislation, there would be an increase of $525,000 a year. The other proposal would have given to Manitoba an extra $650,000 a year.
Looking at the figures for another province where unemployment is high, namely British Columbia, I find that the government's legislation will increase the contribution to that province by $1,150,000. On the other hand, if this 100 per cent payment above the threshold had not been scuttled by the former government and buried by this one the increase in the contribution to British Columbia would be $2,299,894.48, which is considerably more than would be obtained under this legislation. So far as the six participating provinces together are concerned, they will get an additional $2,450,000 as the result of this legislation. If the other proposal had been adopted they would have obtained an additional $5,100,000. That is the sum of those figures the minister gave a few minutes ago.
I am free to admit that in so far as Ontario is concerned, it happens to work out the other way. Apparently in Ontario the situation with regard to employable unemployed is not as serious as it is in Newfoundland, Manitoba and British Columbia. It appears that Ontario will gain more by giving that province 50 per cent under the floor than would be gained by giving an additional 50 per cent over the floor.
Mr. Chairman, we are right back to the principle that we tried to enunciate throughout this whole debate, that unemployment is a national responsibility which flows from economic policies which are the responsibility of the central government. Since this is the case we believe the responsibilities of the federal government should include full responsibility for assistance to employable unemployed wherever they may live in Canada.

I should like to make one or two observations about what the hon. member has said. I said at the beginning that I was going to vote for the bill as it is because it would put more dollars into the treasury of Newfoundland. I stand by that because this is all we are being offered. I quite agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that as an abstract proposition I would find it easier to defend paying 100 per cent above the threshold-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is
this green book abstract?

No, I am not talking about the green book at all. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me to finish my sentence.
Unemployment Assistance Act As an abstract proposition, I would rather support 100 per cent above the threshold than what is proposed by the government because, not merely for monetary reasons but as a matter of principle it seems to me that this threshold was put there by my right hon. friend and was defended by the hon. member for Laurier for the very good reason that the people below the threshold are deemed to be those under public assistance and not unemployed. As a question of principle, it seems to me the hon. gentleman's case is good, and for Manitoba, British Columbia and Newfoundland it would be in a dollar sense better. Of course, the bill the government is proposing is better for Ontario, as the hon. gentleman has pointed out.
What I want to say particularly is that the hon. gentleman has very skilfully-we all know how skilful he is and we all know how difficult it is for a simple person like me to counter his arguments-reversed the whole record. First of all, he talks about the Liberal government having scuttled or having pushed back to the provinces something, as though there had ever been, in the history of this country, a time the federal government in fact had assumed the full cost of unemployment assistance. There never has been.
The first occasion since the war when any responsibility was taken was when it was taken by the Liberal government when the present legislation was enacted which hon. gentlemen opposite are now recommending should be changed. I would remind the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the other members of the committee of one or two facts which the hon. gentleman left out. In the first place, the green book proposal was a proposal for unemployment assistance to be administered and paid for by the federal government; and as a matter of principle the Liberal party has never stood, as fas as I can recall, for paying 100 per cent of the cost of any service administered by someone else. I think that is a thoroughly unsound principle and I would defend that position at any time.
In the second place, the proposal made in 1945 was not that unemployment assistance should be taken over by the federal government as an isolated thing. As I said, it was part of a package deal. It was to be done if the provinces in conference agreed to certain other things which they have never agreed to from that day to this. As a consequence of the failure to reach agreement, the tax rental payments and subsequently the equalization payments were greatly increased; and as a consequence of those greatly increased charges put upon the federal treasury, it was

Unemployment Assistance Act felt by the government, before I became a member of the government and afterwards, that there was no longer the same case that there had been-certainly not the case there had been before the war nor the case there was in 1945-for assuming these charges in two different ways, one by direct tax rental payment into the treasury of the province and then again by assuming the charges in another statute as well.
But on the first occasion on which there was anything more than a very slight amount of seasonal unemployment-and that was the winter of 1954-55-the Liberal government recognized a measure of responsibility and took the initiative in recognizing it, and brought in the legislation with which the hon. gentlemen opposite are now tinkering, and I use the word "tinkering" advisedly. While we have no choice but to accept what they are offering, it is not very much.

In view of what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has just said about tinkering with this question of dealing with unemployment and in view of what he was just saying about the proposals to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been referring, namely the green book proposals, it seems to me that this matter of tinkering is not something which has been initiated with the present administration. I think that what was done in the winter of 1954-55 as a result of seasonal employment could be quite as well described by the use of the word "tinkering", in view of the green book proposal, as what the present administration is doing. However, it seems to me that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, in view of what he was saying, might be interested in having drawn to his attention at this time some words which were used in the debate on the Unemployment Assistance Act by the present Secretary of State. To me at least they point up the fact that while theoretically apparently both the Liberals and the Conservatives have common thinking on this subject, nevertheless all that either of them is prepared to do, when an emergency situation of unemployment arises, is a little bit of tinkering. As found at page 5462 of Hansard of June 28, 1956, the present Secretary of State had this to say. She was speaking following the introduction of the Unemployment Insurance Act by the then minister of national health and welfare and said this:
Having had some experience In municipal affairs I know it is unrealistic to expect the provincial or municipal administrations to be responsible for the administration of this assistance. The government of Canada has set up right across Canada


its own machinery to handle unemployment insurance benefits and it would seem to me that if the government of Canada intends to do something to assist those persons who are not otherwise covered, either by reason of failure to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits because of being in uninsurable employment or by reason of having made insufficient contributions, if the government intends to go along with some sort of assistance it seems to me it could have gone much further than is indicated here in administering these applications.
I would commend those words not only to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate but to the present Minister of National Health and Welfare as an indication of just how far he seems prepared to go in dealing with this matter, as it was advocated by his colleagues in 1956.

I am sure it is useless, Mr. Chairman, ever to try to have the last word in any debate with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. However, I should just like to make an attempt and say that it surely was not tinkering with this problem to get a constitutional amendment and to enact the Unemployment Insurance Act which deals with well over 90 per cent of the problem.

As part of a bargain.

There has been a good deal of history since then, and many aspects of that package deal have been achieved, thanks in part to some of the legislation that my hon. friends placed on the statute books under pressure from certain quarters, as they know.

The other comment I wish to make is that I am still amazed at the stand taken by my Liberal friends with regard to what this legislation actually proposes to do. They say -and say correctly-that what it does is to provide for federal payment of 50 per cent of the cost of maintaining unemployables. The Liberals argue that that is a provincial responsibility and that this legislation, this tinkering with their act, means that the federal government is invading that provincial field. They say they are against it. The hon. member for Laurier said it last night.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

other words, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is voting for something based on a principle to which he is opposed, something he does not believe in, so that he can get the $130,000 for the treasury of Newfoundland. You have no principles.
Oh, oh.

As
far as we are concerned-when the laughter is over-we are prepared to take the same position that my hon. friend's colleague, the member for Essex East took in 1956, when he was the minister of national health and welfare and when he likened this measure to 50 per cent of the pension for the disabled. Pension Act
of the federal government contributing to pensions or allowances for disabled persons, the blind and so on. Likewise we approve of the federal government making a contribution to assistance for unemployables.
