speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 35, to amend the Pension Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, a resolution preliminary to the introduction of Bill 35 was debated a few weeks ago. At that time I explained it was necessary to introduce a bill amending the Pension Act, principally to put into statutory form certain amendments increasing the basic rate pension as amended by the former minister of finance on March 14, 1957, and for which financial provision was made in the statutory estimates by vote No. 670 and Bill No. 418. These increases came into effect July 1, 1957. The bill also provides for additional benefits and brings these benefits more in line with the increases in the basic scale of pensions.

Pension Act
It was also decided to introduce amendments designed to clarify sections of the act in which some doubt regarding interpretation has existed. This is just a tidying up process, mainly to clarify the situation, and which does not infringe in any way on any existing benefits or incur any added liability. At the conclusion of the debate on the resolution, I stated that the observations of hon. members would be studied and I would defer my comments until second reading.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) expressed his concern because, although the proposed amendments would prove to be acceptable, nothing was mentioned about a further increase in the basic scale of pension awards. The present increase just came into effect on July 1 of this year. A brief review of the situation might be helpful. From 1920 to 1947 a 100 per cent pension for a married man was $100 monthly; in 1947 a 100 per cent pension for a married man was increased to $125; in 1952 it was increased to $170 and in 1957 it was increased to $200.
The hon. member for Rosthern, whom I am sorry to see is not here at the moment, was no doubt aware that the Canadian Legion urged a 33J per cent increase last year and the national council-which represents the amps, blind, paraplegics, army, navy and air force veterans, Canadian corps association, Hong Kong veterans, etc.-requested in February 1957 "that the basic rate of pension,
i.e., war disability compensation for 100 per cent disability be increased to at least double the 1939 rate". As a matter of fact the request was implemented on July 1 of this year. The Legion, in a brief presented to the cabinet, a copy of which has been circulated to each hon. member, upheld a short time ago its request that the increase be 33J per cent and that is the subject of close study in the light of other governing factors.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Macdonald) was another who expressed his disappointment at there being no increase in the basic scale and suggested the scale had gone behind the cost of living in other indices. That again illustrates the need of further study and reference to a committee on veterans affairs as has happened in the past and, might I state from my own personal knowledge, took up considerable time in past committees. He also observed that when a disability pensioner entered into a common law union after his discharge from service some consideration should be given on behalf of his partner. He suggested our divorce laws were medieval. This is a situation which I would not desire to discuss any further at this stage, but it illustrates the need for an examination by a committee.

The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway also claimed that British disability pensioners who came to Canada after discharge had no rights under the Pension Act and suggested they were deserving cases. Canada does supplement the awards of Canadians with prewar domicile who served in the forces of Her Majesty or Her Majesty's allies but has never accepted the principle that such pensioners who had no pre-war residence and came to Canada for the first time after discharge from service with their own country are entitled to that benefit.
The hon. member wished some clarification regarding the award of pension and other allowances to paraplegics. The Canadian pension commission assesses the disability from paraplegia as total and pays a pension at 100 per cent. In addition thereto, the commission pays a helplessness allowance as provided in section 30 (1) of the act. This allowance varied from a minimum of $480 per annum to a maximum of $1,400, and the latter amount was increased to $1,800 from July 1, 1957. This increase was granted on the urgent representations of the commission to provide for a group of helpless pensioners who required constant attendance day and night, the majority being bedridden. The commission revised their table of disabilities as of July 1, 1957, to provide for the following four classifications under which helplessness allowance is paid:
Constant
A bedridden case or equivalent who requires constant nursing care and attendance in his home, $1,800 per annum.
Almost Constant
Cases totally disabled and helpless who require a great deal of attendance, particularly during the day, $1,440 per annum.
Intermittent attendance-day and night
This degree of attendance is self-explanatory,

Occasional attendance during the day
This degree of attendance is self-explanatory,

Paraplegics, prior to July 1, 1957, received $1,400 and, unless they require constant attendance in their homes day and night, are classed as almost constant and paid now at $1,440.
I might state that earlier this month I met a delegation of the paraplegic association from Toronto and Montreal who, quite frankly, were of the opinion they should receive the maximum award of helplessness allowance of $1,800 and their representations are now being studied. However, the actual amount to be paid is subject to the decision of the commission, which is charged with sole responsibility and jurisdiction. This is another subject which should be studied by a parliamentary committee.

The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo also stated the life certificates issued by the commission were misleading and that pensioners were not aware they could claim the continuation of additional pension for children who were continuing their education after attaining the statutory age limitation of 16 or 17. This statement resulted in an immediate inquiry, because the commission has always maintained its responsibility is to provide the maximum benefits permissible by the statute. When a child reaches the statutory age limitation for pension, the chief treasury officer sends out a statement on form 250-B, showing the adjustment of pension. Accompanying this is a form letter, over the signature of the chairman, which quotes the act, gives information regarding the additional pension under section 26(1) (a) and (b), and instructs the pensioner what to do.
Frankly, I do not see what more the commission can do, as pensioners are encouraged at all times to make application on behalf of these children. A further letter of advice goes with the adjustment cheque when pension for the child is continued beyond the statutory age limitation.

There were certain provisions made for the merchant seamen, but possibly there has not been as much done for them as there should have been. This matter also should receive study by a committee when one is set up.
The hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. McLeod) stated it was not unusual to find the same members on the appeal board as had adjudicated on the original decision. This is not the case, and would be in direct violation of section 60 (5) (c), which states:
That no member of an appeal board of the commission shall adjudicate upon any case coming before an appeal board pursuant to this section, if such member has previously sat as a member of the commission at any hearing of such case, as herein provided, unless the applicant's consent thereto has first been obtained.
An appeal board consists of three members, and two boards sit in different parts of Canada each week. Occasionally one member of the board may have adjudicated upon the claim previously. If so, the applicant is advised by his advocate and, if he refuses to give his consent, the hearing is deferred.
The same hon. member stated it was almost impossible to have the decision of the commission modified by the appeal board. Actually, the reverse is true, as will be found on page 63 of the annual report of my department for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1957:
Number of claims heard by the appeal
boards during the year	 1,510
Number of claims granted by the appeal
boards during the year	 624
Number of claims not granted	 752
The balance of 134 were pending, struck off or withdrawn. Further, if the hon. member will refer to page 69 of the same report he will find what, hanoened to all the world war

Pension Act
I applications for pension received during the year and, on page 83, what happened to the world war II applications. He will be surprised to see the number granted on first application, and those on further hearing or renewal after the presentation of additional evidence without the necessity of going to appeal.
The hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Thomas) asked how the commission reaches decisions regarding entitlement in cases where an applicant was enlisted as category A and discharged in a lower category; how does the commission disclaim responsibility? This involves a question, Mr. Speaker, which has on many occasions been the subject of discussion in this house and before committees on veterans affairs. I must say that when the Canadian pension commission renders a decision, it states the reasons leading thereto and the sources are open to the applicant should he desire to proceed further with his claim. Also, there is a branch of my department called the veterans' bureau, which is staffed with qualified personnel who are able to advise applicants, without cost, as to their claims. Parliament has charged the commission with sole responsibility in all matters relating to the adjudication and award of pension. I have taken careful note regarding the observations of my hon. friend, which are by no means new, and know full well that this subject of preenlistment conditions will be fully explored by the first committee of this house to deal with the Pension Act.
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) made particular mention of the fire fighters. Considerable study was given by previous committees of this house to the problems of the fire fighters. We have the Fire Fighters War Service Benefits Act making special provision for the fire fighters and they also get special attention under the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. There will be further study if it is felt something more is needed.
In closing with these general observations, Mr. Speaker, I desire to thank hon. members for their constructive criticism all of which will be studied and which, may I state again, points out the need for a careful study and review of pension legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say that this group welcomes this amending bill as it does bring forward some worth-while amendments to the Pension Act. Although there are a number of omissions so far as the representations made by the Canadian Legion and the National Council of Veterans are concerned,

nevertheless the amendments are all to the good. I have been nice up to this point but I am going to be nasty from now on.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not believe you can be nasty.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
The last time I spoke about veterans affairs I made the statement that needy veterans were being denied admission to hospitals of the Department of Veterans Affairs in Canada. I made that statement as the result of a visit to Shaughnessy hospital in Vancouver, meeting veterans and their parents and information given me at Legion meetings. Since I made that statement I have received a lot of correspondence particularly from the coastal cities of British Columbia supporting my contention.
I am not one given to making exaggerated statements. I try to get the facts before I make a statement and I am one who does not relish his word being challenged. Therefore I am going to deal with one particular letter which I have received which definitely proves my case. Many of these old boys cut clippings out the Vancouver Province or the Vancouver Sun commenting on my previous statement and send them to me. One of such clippings reads as follows:
DVA Denies Veterans Not Looked After-
A charge in the commons at Ottawa that male immigrants are getting treatment at Shaughnessy hospital while "war veterans are denied admission" was denied here.
"At no time has an entitled veteran been refused admission to treatment," William Roaf, western regional administrator for the veterans affairs department said.
The protest against "needy veterans" being turned away from the military hospital while male immigrants were receiving hospital services, dentures, and glasses, was made in the commons by C.C.F. member for Kootenay West, H. W. Herridge.
That was my contention, Mr. Speaker. I am not blaming any of the officials or anyone in the department. I know that no eligible veteran has been denied treatment but I can prove that needy and destitute veterans knocking on the door of Shaughnessy hospital have been denied admission while immigrants and others were being well taken care of.
I am going to quote from the letter to which I referred earlier which indicates that my protest was quite correct based on the experience of the author of the letter. This man writes saying that he has a wife and three children depending on him. He has been unemployed since November 1956, received no unemployment insurance benefits and no relief but is in receipt of a pension of 20 per cent. His private doctor has informed him that both his feet are infected and that at age 58 the chances of recovery are indeed very remote and if something is not done

immediately amputation may be required. He indicates that he applied to Shaughnessy for further treatment and was denied it, he got the brushoff. He writes:
I am out of work. I have no money. The Department of Veterans Affairs are or seem to be reluctant about giving me the necessary treatment. They won't admit me to hospital.
He goes on to say that because of his unemployment he is suffering from starvation and also a lack of medical treatment. The man gives his complete history here and outlines the difficulties he has encountered since he returned from the war. I use this as an illustration to prove my contention is correct. I have a file here on my desk containing many similar letters.

I realize they have to be looked after but it causes a lot of discontent and ill-feeling when you find that veterans have been denied admission to the departmental hospital while immigrants are well cared for. I know the minister's officials do what they can to have
Pension Act
veterans looked after by some provincial institution and so on but that is not good enough. The veteran has a first right to be given treatment in Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals. I know that the minister's heart is in the right place in these matters. I urge that he have this situation looked into and urgently have the regulations amended, a course of action which I think is necessary, so these needy cases can be cared for.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
As I said before, the bill is welcomed by this group as offering a number of improvements but there are some omissions with which I want to deal. I am sure the minister will support me 100 per cent in the first omission I am going to discuss because we stood together in support of this omission in the past. I refer to the question of increasing the rates payable under the Pension Act by 33J per cent. I do not want to take the time of the house to deal with it at length. I think the shortest way to deal with it would be to put on the record the opinion of the Canadian Legion as expressed in the brief presented to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the cabinet in November 1957. This outlines the situation very well indeed, as follows:
Historically, the scale of pensions was related to the common labour market. Some examples from the above tables show that this is no longer the case and that pension rates have failed to keep pace with the salaries and wages paid in the forces, the civil service and industry:-
(1)	Cleaner and helper, one of the lower paid brackets in the civil service receive $300 less than a married 100 per cent pensioner in 1920. Today such a worker receives $510 more. His wages have increased over 223 per cent, the married pensioner's rate only 100 per cent.
(2)	It should be noted that the rates shown on the chart for a private soldier are those which apply to an untrained recruit on entry. He may after four months' service, if he reaches the required standard of competency, get a further $72 per annum; after an additional 12 months he may get another $156 per annum. These increases are for the untrained soldier but do not take into account group pay for which tradesmen may be eligible. Thus a private soldier with 13 months' service and no previous experience would, if married, get $2,928 per annum as compared with $2,400 for a 100 per cent disability married pensioner.
(3)	The wage index reflecting the rates paid workers in industry (logging, mining, manufacturing, trade, transportation, construction, light and power and personal services) shows that since 1920

Pension Act
the index has risen from 52.3 to 149.4 in 1956, which is an increase of approximately 185 per cent, whilst in the same period the rate for a married 100 per cent pensioner has risen only 100 per cent.
There is no question but that the standard of living as illustrated in these groups has permanently improved.
And we are all glad of it.
We submit that with due regard to all the difficulties of exact comparison, these figures indicate the necessity of an upward revision of the pension rates. This should be at least 33', per cent over the 1956 rates in order to bring them more into line with the substantial increase in general wage rates in recent years. The Canadian Legion therefore recommends that the rates payable under schedules "A" and "B" of the Canadian Pension Act as of June 30, 1957 be increased by 33J per cent.
I am quite sure the minister has not changed his mind on this matter in a period of 18 months or two years and I do urge that consideration be given to these representations when further amendments to the act are considered. Then there is another amendment lacking which the minister will remember was the subject of considerable discussion in the veterans affairs committee on a number of occasions. That is the one having to do with conditions not recorded on enlistment. If my memory serves me correctly, the minister was very keen on an amendment of this type being placed in the act in order to correct what he, with other members of the committee, considered was an injustice. The brief has something to say about this question and I am going to quote it because the Legion spent a lot of time in drafting it and have presented the case well with an economy of words. This is what the brief has to say on page 13:
We request that section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that, where a pension applicant who served in an actual threatre of war is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or a disease not recorded on medical examination made on enlistment or prior thereto, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or had its inception subsequent to enlistment.
Whether a recruit is taken from the comparative protection of civilian life and subjected to the dangers and rigours of military life is determined by government regulation. The government, for the purpose of determining whether the recruit is physically fit and is to be accepted, gives him a medical examination. The nature and extent of such examination is under the sole control of the state. The examination is very comprehensive and rigorous. The findings are recorded. On the basis of such findings the government determines whether the recruit is to be accepted for military service and whether he is to be subjected to conditions of service in a theatre of war. Having full control of the recruiting and the character and place of the recruit's subsequent service, the government should abide, for pension purposes, by its recorded findings in such medical examination, supplemented by actual medical records in existence prior to enlistment.

How many times members of the committee made use of that argument throughout the years.
This is not so under section 13 (1) (a). Many war disabled veterans notwithstanding the ameliorating provisions of section 13 (1) (c) undoubtedly are denied pensions which they would receive if the government were to abide by the results of medical examination on enlistment or pre-enlistment medical records. This situation is particularly acute in cases involving mental or nervous conditions.
I have had one or two in that category brought to my attention.
The Legion submits that the Pension Act should be changed so that Canada's obligation will be honoured. The Canadian Legion therefore recommends that section 13 (1) (a) of the Pension Act be amended so that, where a pension applicant who served in an actual theatre of war is found to have a disability resulting from an injury or a disease not recorded on medical examination prior to enlistment, such injury or disease shall be presumed to have occurred or had its inception subsequent to enlistment.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we do not want to be unfair. We cannot expect everything to be done overnight by a government that has just recently taken office but the minister knows this has been the cause of considerable discontent and debate in the veterans affairs committee in past years and on behalf of this group I do urge him to give further consideration to this recommendation of the Canadian Legion, a recommendation which has been brought forward year after year because of the experience of the members of the Legion with the situation as it exists throughout the country.
There is another deficiency having to do with retroactive awards under section 31. Here is a matter that has also been dealt with by the committee from time to time and the minister knows the story just as well as I do. I am going to quote again from the Legion brief because I can say more in a few words.
We would advocate that it be made mandatory that when a decision is given favourable to the veteran, pension will be paid as of date of application. At present this is a matter which is left to the discretion of the Canadian pension commission, but section 31 (1) of the act limits the discretion to a maximum of 12 months. Section 31 (2) permits an additional six months when hardship and distress would otherwise occur, and section 31	(3) permits an additional 18 months
pension where there are administrative delays beyond the applicant's control.
I think the commission has administered this section of the act very fairly indeed.
For a number of years after world war I pensions when granted became retroactive to the appearance of the disability or sometimes the date of discharge. As a result some awards involved large retroactive payments and it was argued that this fact made the commission extremely reluctant to grant the application. To do away with this psychological barrier a practical injustice was permitted in order

to secure a more unbiased consideration of the merits of the applicant's claim without being unduly influenced by the financial consequences of a favourable decision.
Experience, however, has shown that there are many cases of delay beyond the applicant's control which often result, under present regulations, in both injustice and hardship. We believe that the adoption of our recommendation will go a long way to rectify these abuses. . . . The Canadian Legion therefore recommends that all disability pensions when granted become effective from the date of application, but in order to allay fears of excessive awards going back to world war I jeopardizing the chances of the applicant, we append the following saving clause:
"This provision shall not apply to claims granted prior to January 1, 1946, and no retroactive payments shall be made for a period prior to that date."
I trust the minister will give that recommendation some consideration. I know that the present provisions of the act were finally-placed in the act as the result of considerable discussion in the veterans affairs committee and representations by members of the commission and others. The Legion feels there is still a measure of injustice under the application of the present section.
I want to deal now with a section which is termed "Debts Due to the Crown" because I have had a few cases of this sort brought to my attention. While they are not frequent, on occasion there is some difficulty and some injustice done the veteran because of the present legislation.
The Canadian Legion has information indicating that it is the policy of the treasury board, where a veteran is in receipt of pension with respect to a disability attributable to military service and the Canadian government has a money claim against the veteran, to authorize the deduction of the amount of such claim from the veteran's disability pension. The Minister of Finance upon receiving such authorization thereupon makes the deduction.
The alleged basis of the above-mentioned procedure is section 95 (1) of the Financial Administration Act, which provides for the crown setting off a debt to it against a debt by the crown to its creditor.
We are confident that parliament did not have veterans' pensions in mind when it enacted section 95 (1) of the Financial Administration Act, and, moreover, that it would not have enacted that section in its present form if it had been informed that the section would be used to deprive veterans of their pension benefits.
We urge that the crown's obligation to make monthly payments under an award of the pension commission is not an ordinary debt such as is contemplated by section 95 (1) of the Financial Administration Act.
It is something different and of a much higher character. It is a moral obligation of Canada, acknowledged by the nation through its own tribunal, the Canadian pension commission, to ensure that the hardship to the pensioner resulting from his disability incurred in the service of his country shall be minimized. Having assumed that obligation the nation is, in the Legion's view, bound not to disavow it.
Parliament has declared by section 24 (3), formerly section 20 (3) of the Pension Act, that a pension may not be attached. The Canadian Legion says that this is a statutory confirmation of the special character of Canada's obligation to its
Pension Act
disabled veterans. It is essentially a debt of honour. Parliament has in effect said and decreed that money payments arising out of that obligation must not be diverted from their purpose, that of ameliorating financial hardship arising out of war disability.
The Legion submits that the Canadian government is bound, if not legally then morally, by section 24 (3) of the Pension Act.
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends:
That in order to obviate all possibility of future diversion of war pensions section 24 (3) be amended so that it will specifically bind the crown.
Why should the crown not be bound in this respect when ordinary individuals or corporations are bound. I believe there is a section of the act that certainly should be amended according to the recommendation of the Legion.
I have a final complaint. I told the minister I was going to be a bit nasty this afternoon. My complaint is in connection with marital status under the act. I had a case recently which particularly brought to my attention the necessity for some amendment to this section of the act. The cases are relatively few in percentage, but very often innocent people are the victims of circumstances over which they had no control. In that connection the Legion has this to say:
There are Canadian pensioners and widows of deceased pensioners who have lost pension rights because of their marital status. In these cases either the man or the woman was married peviously and obtained a divorce outside of Canada which is not recognized under Canadian law.
I dealt with a case like that just last month.
Therefore the second form of marriage is held to be improper by the Canadian pension commission which refuses to recognize the wife for purposes of additional pension, and when the man dies it similarly refuses to recognize the widow. In some cases the commission has previously recognized the woman and paid additional pension during the man's lifetime and then after his death discovered the invalid divorce and refused to recognize the widow. The commission has exercised its discretion in some cases but there is evidence that it does not always do so.
There are other instances where a separation has occurred and as a result there is an impediment to marriage creating a situation comparable to an unrecognized divorce.
There are not many of these cases but those that have come to our attention have been tragic.
That has been my experience.
With respect to those that result from an unrecognized divorce there is little doubt but that the parties concerned acted in good faith and felt that they were free to remarry.
The commission, following a meeting in January 1955, asked the Legion what is could suggest as a remedy to this problem.
This is their suggestion:
We believe that it could be remedied by a provision similar to section 30 (11) (b) of the War Veterans Allowance Act, but worded so as to take care of the widows also. . . .
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends: That a clause similar to section 30 (11) (b) of the War Veterans Allowance Act be included in the Canadian Pension Act, and further, that this clause be so worded as to provide for the widow.

Unemployment Assistance Act
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I said when commencing my few remarks, we in this group welcome the amendments provided in this bill, but we also urge the minister to give consideration to the other representations of the Canadian Legion. There is only one representation, sir, that will affect a large number of people, and that is the one asking for a 33J per cent increase in the basic pension rate. The other amendments that I have outlined affect relatively few people, but the people affected are entitled to justice as well as the larger number, and the present act causes a certain injustice in those cases. On behalf of this group, I do ask the minister in the time between now and the next session to give serious consideration to these representations and give effect to his own previously expressed wishes by amending the act to meet the requests of the Canadian Legion.

I had asked the minister what the attitude of the province of Quebec was with reference to the resolu-

I wonder if he could say, when he rises, whether or not any negotiations or any discussions have taken place between the two bodies leading to an agreement.
While I am on my feet I should like to clarify the attitude which I adopted last night in discussing this matter. I did not think it was necessary to do that because surely it is possible for an hon. member to get up and question certain parts of a bill without, for that reason, being opposed to it. Next, my position and certainly the position of this side of the house, was clearly indicated when we assured the minister that we were willing at once, following disposal of the resolution, to move on to second reading of the bill. This is indicative of an attitude of co-operation and not one of opposition.
This leads me to the statement that there is no difficulty about my position, which is that of supporting the bill and voting for the bill, because it is going to increase the contributions to the provincial governments. The point I was making was that because of the amendment which was made to the British North America Act which authorized the federal government to enter into the field of unemployment insurance, that did not authorize the federal government to enter into the field of unemployment assistance. In that case I feel, as I am sure most hon. members on this side of the house feel, that for that reason this bill is an impingement upon provincial rights.
I do not want to repeat what I said last night but it strikes me that there can be no doubt about that, not only because of the constitutional position as it stands today but I am sure most hon. members who have given this matter any thought would feel that way about the matter. But what amazed me more than anything else was that the province of Quebec which as a rule takes quite a strong stand against the infringement of provincial rights would, through the head of its delegation at the provincial conference, as I understand it did, adopt the position that the federal government should go all the way and pay all of unemployment assistance.
I thought I should make these points. They should not be surprising to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Surely it is possible to say in the house that one is against certain views. Surely it is possible to say that a bill infringes upon provincial rights and still support it because

of the fact that the provinces and incidentally the municipalities are going to be assisted. My position also was brought about by the fact that during the campaign some fairly strong statements were made as well as prior to the campaign over a period of years, by the former leader of the opposition and other hon. members who now sit on the other side of the house, to the effect that there would be a positive decentralization of these matters if they took office. It strikes me that in this case there is just the contrary. There is a tendency to invade the field of public assistance, leaving very little in that field other than perhaps mothers' allowances and several other smaller matters. For that reason it seems to me that the position which I have taken is quite tenable.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we had a debate on this matter at the resolution stage. In the meantime we had a chance to look at the bill and I do not think it is necessary to debate it at length at this stage. One of my colleagues has a few remarks of a general character which he will be making while Your Honour is in the chair, but our position is clear. We feel that there is nothing wrong about federal assistance to the provinces in fields such as moneys for disabled persons, blindness allowances and other such measures. Accordingly we do not see that it is wrong for the federal government to assist the provinces in the field of assistance to the unemployable unemployed. We therefore have no difficulty in voting for this measure. We are also prepared to vote for it because it puts a few more dollars into the provincial treasuries.
I confess that I am still amazed at the position taken by my friend the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). There is nothing else that this bill does but to provide money to assist the provinces in their payments to the unemployable unemployed. If he thinks that is an infringement upon provincial responsibility it seems to me that his course should be to vote against the measure. But since we are for it, I am glad to know that everybody else is for it as well. Nevertheless we think we express the disappointment of the Canadian people that, after all these years during which it has been contended in many quarters that there should be 100 per cent federal responsibility for the employable unemployed that contention is still not being implemented in the legislation that is now before us. We hope that even yet we may reach that point. I am glad to hear that my hon. friends of the Liberal party now say that they still take that position. I hope that between us we may yet be able to persuade
Unemployment Assistance Act the government to go that far as well. Nevertheless, as we have already made clear at the resolution stage, we support this legislation as far as it goes.

Mr. Speaker, so far the discussion, chiefly on the resolution stage, has dealt with the technical implications in this proposed resolution. I do not wish to get involved in that particular part of the debate because there are others who are far more capable of investigating the technical fields. However, I was glad to hear the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) somewhat shift his ground, as we reached second reading of the bill, from the position he had taken earlier. I was becoming concerned, on hearing him talk about the invasion of provincial rights, because it is rather unusual to find an hon. member from his party taking a position politically to the right of the premier of Quebec. I was afraid that he was quickly going to become the sole surviving Canadian Dixiecrat of the Canadian House of Commons. But apparently he is prepared to go along with this bill at this time.
The point I wanted to raise at this particular juncture of the debate is that we are in danger of losing sight of the chief objective or the chief purpose toward which this parliament should be working with regard to employment. Certainly we are in favour of doing everything possible-whether it is at the federal level, the provincial level or the municipal level or any combination thereof-to alleviate the effects of unemployment and to do something to alleviate the suffering that may result from prolonged periods of unemployment. But I am afraid that this is the kind of legislation which, as I am sure you will agree, Mr. Speaker, we all hope will not be required. I think we all believe that it would be far more desirable if we could do something to keep the level of employment in such a state that not only would there not be any crisis in unemployment but that even the .45 formula would not have to come up for consideration.
The present situation seems to be, on the basis of the latest figures, that we are approaching very rapidly a figure of 400,000 unemployed in this country. I wonder if we assess the full significance of what is happening. On a very conservative estimate, -and I use the word conservative with a small "c" there-if there are 400,000 unemployed, and if the loss in work that could be performed or products that could be produced were taken conservatively at $10 a day- and that in this day is a very small figure- that would be a loss of $4 million a day,

Unemployment Assistance Act which would come to approximately $120 million a month. That figure in itself indicates how costly and expensive unemployment can be. That is taking into consideration only the financial side of it. When we take into consideration the human side of it,- the uncertainty, the fears, the doubts and the worries that go along with unemployment and what it does to the average family- then of course the cost is incalculable.
I am wondering why the government has not, even in the course of this debate or at any previous time when unemployment was being discussed, made some announcement of some long range plan, something more imaginative and bold than has been indicated by the previous administration or so far by this administration. I am thinking of something like the setting up of a national employment commission which would lay the emphasis not on looking after the unemployed but on providing the widest possible opportunity for employment. In other words, they \yould look at the positive side of this question rather than the negative results. I believe a commission of that nature could be very useful and could do a great deal in co-operation with the provinces and the municipalities. Certainly if such a commission were set up and were given authority by this parliament to enter into negotiations, discussions and agreements with the provinces and the municipalities, in my view that would be one of the finest and easiest ways of overcoming this continuing argument that comes up again and again as to who enters into another field of endeavour, and the question of infringing upon provincial rights or provincial autonomy.
I say this because an agreement of that nature would mean that under the terms of this bill they would be empowered by negotiation and agreement to enter into public works and long-range plans and winter employment programs with the provinces and municipalities, provided that the financial basis upon which to make all those things possible was provided by this parliament. I think it would grip the imagination of the Canadian people and would give us a sense of national enterprise which I think is lacking today.
I have been in this house for a considerable number of years now and have heard hundreds of debates and arguments about public enterprise and private enterprise and the relative virtues of the two or the virtues of one as opposed to the other, but I have never heard any member of the government bring forward an imaginative program which we could call a national enterprise in which there would be room for public enterprise, private


enterprise and co-operative enterprise, but with the emphasis on enterprise. I believe we have the kind of country which needs that kind of leadership and that type of leadership would result in the minimum need of this kind of legislation.
To give an example of what such a national commission could do, I might take the suggestion which was made by a member who was on this side of the house, I believe last year or two years ago. That member was the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) who is now one of the parliamentary assistants on the government side. At that time he brought in a resolution to deal with the dispersal of industry and he pointed out that there was a potential for small processing and manufacturing industries, particularly but not exclusively in western Canada. The possibilities, of course, are great both to the east and to the west of our national capital and this is a time when I believe the hon. member for Brandon-Souris would be doing a great national service if he would put these arguments and ideas before the government and bring them to the attention of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill), and try to persuade them to take some positive steps along those lines in the near future.
Statistics show that in the last six years there have been almost 50,000 farmers who have left their lands-that is taking the whole area right across Canada. On the prairies the process has been perhaps more speedy than in any other province. We are losing our farm population by the thousands in every one of our rural communities in western Canada. Now I may be asked "what has that to do with this legislation?" It has this to do with it. Every time a farmer leaves his land and goes into the city to seek employment he is creating more than the normal employment problem. In the average farm family there would be more than one working adult and as long as they stay on the farm they are not in the labour market. They are their own employers but, the minute they leave that farm and enter the city they have in my opinion made a very fatal decision because they have decided to stop being their own employers and to throw themselves on the mercy of some other employer. Now I am not critical of such persons as they may do so as a matter of necessity or as a matter of choice, but it is a process which has been going on and which is going on and which I believe is a very dangerous process if we should run into any further unemployment difficulties.
Now, if we had small manufacturing and processing industries dispersed throughout our

farming areas, particularly in the prairie provinces where we do not at the present time have many such industries, many of which have to be planned and initiated by such a planning commission as I have described and perhaps even initially financed by the federal government, this would in my opinion be a sound investment.
Small industries would have a stabilizing effect in keeping farm families on the farm. It is well known there are many farms today, I believe, particularly in the province of Quebec, where the people would not be living on the farm at all since the land is not capable of sustaining a sufficient income if it were not that they lived somewhere in the vicinity of a pulp mill, paper mill or a mine of some kind where they may obtain parttime if not full-time employment. This makes it possible for them to stay at home on the farm and supplement their farm income with a certain amount of income from employment in industry.
Now in western Canada such a program is particularly important and would have very beneficial results which would help to stem this tide of families leaving the farms and seeking employment in industrial areas, thus boosting the large unemployment figures. At the same time it would make it possible for those who find it difficult to maintain themselves on a farm income to do part-time work in the off-season period so far as farms are concerned and would enable them to earn sufficient extra income to keep their families together, maintain themselves, and stay on the land.
Apart from the opportunities I have outlined, I would like to draw the attention of the government to the obvious opportunities before us that were mentioned the other day in another context. It does seem rather strange, and in fact a little ridiculous, that a country such as ours where no one seems to think we lack resources, the physical capacity to produce or even financial resources, that we are not somehow able to relate the financial and the physical possibilities in order to provide full employment and full production in our country.
As I have already pointed out, we are losing approximately $4 million worth of labour per day as a result of unemployment at the present time, over $100 million a month. If that amount of money were to be put into useful public works projects-and I am not talking merely about providing employment per se but providing employment through socially useful public works projects -we would be recovering that money in a valuable way. If the government wants some ideas as to where such employment could be
Unemployment Assistance Act found or what could be done, I will give them a few recommendations or suggestions.
If they would look at recent reports on the position of our educational facilities across Canada I think they would find there is a tremendous need for school construction. As a former schoolteacher I can assure the house that I have followed the position of our educational facilities very closely, even though I am no longer active in that field, and I find there is a tremendous amount of replacement to be done. There are many small school-houses, built 40 or 50 years ago, which ought to be replaced with buildings having modern facilities. The same might be said of many of our hospitals and other public institutions which are crying out for replacement. The materials are there and labour apparently is there, almost 400,000 men. Somehow the government up to this time, however, has failed to relate these two things and to produce the socially necessary institutions.
There are many demands in every province in this country of ours and yet we do not have full employment at the present time. It is not something that needs any great amount of planning or great technicians or scientists; all it needs is a little bit of common sense and then we can get right down to work.
I mentioned the other day in a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Hamilton) the question of houses on our Indian reservations. I do not refer to the reservations in eastern Canada but those in my own province.
I happen to have five Indian reservations in my own constituency, and I can say that the housing conditions of most of them are disgraceful. Many of them are living in log shacks, shacks which are broken down and no longer suitable as residences, and at least a few of these Indians happen to be right alongside large sawmills where there is a huge surplus of lumber waiting to be sold. At the same time there is unemployment in the area, yet somehow the government cannot manage to relate this raw material this available labour and these log shacks and provide the Indians with decent frame houses in which to live in some measure of comfort. This is one of the things which could be done right away to bring a measure of relief to the situation.
And what about homes for our senior citizens? What about schools for the technical training of our young people? News stories have appeared recently showing how far behind this country has fallen in relation to the training of scientists. Here is a field which could be tackled right away. Let us provide the facilities to give our young people

Unemployment Assistance Act the education and the technical training to fit them for the new kind of world in which we are living and in which we are likely to be living in the future.
These are random ideas, Mr. Speaker, but the main thought I should like to leave with the government is this: it is nothing short of ridiculous to have a position where we are losing approximately $4 million worth of labour a day, and in which there are thousands of things to be done at a time when we have all the materials necessary to do these things and plenty of resources behind those materials to replace them when they are used. I know that this government is firmly attached to the idea that private enterprise can do everything, but let them swallow their pride to some extent, throw that book away and say that what is required now is a little imagination and the use of all forms of enterprise. If this is done I think we will reach the stage when this type of legislation will no longer be required.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on this bill. First of all, I want to commend the government for this alleviation of unemployment. I also would like to say that in view of the conditions now developing in Canada, I think this government should make a still greater effort toward a solution of the problem.
One of my saddest experiences has indeed been to see how many people come to us in our offices asking for jobs because they don't qualify for unemployment benefits.
I do not know who was saying some years ago that the mortal sin of democracy was to let people be unemployed. Our society is responsible for the unemployment of the labouring masses who were attracted to the cities by industries that later left them jobless.
According to figures given by an association which met recently with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), there are at present
800,000	people who do not come under the Unemployment Insurance Act. That is over 10 per cent of our labour force. In rural districts like mine, this proportion is even greater in these difficult times.
I therefore commend the government for improving the act, but I do regret that it did not do more. I understood it was going to introduce far-reaching reforms not only in unemployment insurance, but in our social system in general, since it claimed to be filled with good intentions.
As for me, whatever government may be in power, I will never fail to approve of any
LMr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).]

legislation providing help for those who have to rely on public assistance.
I have already said that legislation stands in need of continued improvement. I feel that at this time, because of the unemployment which is far more acute this year than anything we have known since the war, we should be prepared to do more.
I have attempted to understand this problem of unemployment by looking at statistics. If I look at the monthly bulletin put out by the Labour Gazette I must admit that the information provided there is unfortunately altogether incomplete. We are given figures about men at work, we are told how many claims there have been for unemployment insurance benefits, the amount of claims allowed and so on, but we are not told how many unemployed do not qualify for benefits. How many unemployed are at this time not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits? We know nothing about it. To understand perfectly the problem of unemployment as it exists in this country, the Labour Gazette should publish fuller information. All we can do about this matter at this time is to act on feeling alone, knowing nothing of the basic factors of the problem.
Newspaper reports tell us that at the present time there are 392,000 unemployed. How many of those people do not receive unemployment benefits?
Moreover, there is confusion, as was stated quite often in the past, between statistics of the dominion bureau of statistics and those of the unemployment insurance commission. One thing is certain. It is that the unemployed care little about statistics. That is what happened not so long ago in Vancouver when a Conservative member tried to explain to
1,000	unemployed people that, owing to the present policy of the government, there was more work available than last year. These people replied: "What do we care about your statistics, give us jobs."
If we are to maintain the prestige and value of our democratic system, the government must take strong measures, even if it has to resort to deficit budgeting. Its first duty is to fight unemployment efficiently.
Recently two hundred Hungarians clamoured to be sent back home because they had failed to find in Canada the jobs they had a right to expect. Today the first right of man, after his right to live, is the right to work. In my own country, I see healthy people of 45 or 50 years of age who are jobless.
People at 65, in perfect health, who could still be useful to society cannot find jobs; qualified engineers with an experience of 10 or 15 years, at a time when we complain

about a shortage of engineers in Canada, are turned down because industry cannot pay them a decent salary. I am therefore inclined to think that there is something wrong with our system. I take this opportunity to urge our national authorities to assume their responsibilities instead of being satisfied with half measures.
What I am saying today, I have said before; I have always held the same opinion. A country as rich as ours; one of the leading democratic countries which now sets itself as an example for other countries by its broad-mindedness and its tolerance; a country anxious to take an important part in international affairs, must start by putting its own house in order. This unemployment problem being extremely important, we must strive first and foremost to find a solution to it. Any government which can solve that problem shall deserve our gratitude.

This question as to whether or not there was adequate consultation with the provinces before this proposal in the schedule to this bill was brought into parliament I think has some rather interesting aspects. The minister says that it is a good proposition. He suggests that it is so good that anybody would be foolish not to take it. Nevertheless I do not see that anything he has done in this connection gives him, the hon. member for Peel or anybody else over there on the opposite side of the house, any right to claim that the course of action that has been pursued by the administration is very much different from the sort of action that was pursued by the members who are now in the official opposition when they were carrying on negotiations with the provinces. Sitting over here where I do in the C.C.F. corner of the house perhaps I can say this, because I might be considered an impartial observer as to the activities of the Liberal party and the Conservative party and their relative merits.
Merits?

Or lack of merits. My colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo, with his usual astuteness, suggests there is perhaps not as much merit in the actions of either of them as they would like to suggest there is.
There is one aspect of this matter which is implicit in the schedule to the bill which we
IMr. Barnett.]
have before us, as it was in the schedule to the original Old Age Assistance Act that came before this house, and which has yet not been touched upon. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the official opposition spoke extensively on this bill when it was before this house earlier at the resolution stage. We do not now propose to add to or to repeat the representations which we made at that time. We do however wish to confirm our support of this bill and to say at the same time that we feel further changes are necessary in the veterans' legislation in order to embody those representations which have been made from this side of the house and also from veterans' organizations.
The spirit of our veterans' legislation is that the veteran should always be given the benefit of doubt. Many of us have come across cases which would seem to indicate that the law is administered in accordance with the letter rather than the spirit and consequently the veterans are deprived of the benefit of doubt.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned this afternoon cases of disability where the condition had been ruled to have existed prior to enlistment. We feel that any veteran who was accepted by the medical authorities on behalf of the government and inducted into any of the armed services must be given the benefit of doubt, and whether any condition existed or not, the fact that the government accepted him in that condition
Pension Act
necessitates that the government should therefore accept responsibility and rule that any condition developing afterwards was attributable to his service.
There are other cases where veterans developed conditions during service which necessitated surgical operation. Sometimes many years after his discharge another condition develops which is not related to the condition for which the operation was performed, but to the operation itself. We feel that in such cases the veteran should also receive the benefit of doubt.
There are cases of cancer development, hypertensional blood pressure, all of which developed in postwar years many years after the veteran was discharged and which have been attributed to pre-enlisted conditions. We feel in such cases they should be ruled as resulting from service.
There are also cases such as mental and nervous disorders which often develop after discharge and, in view of the hardships, the stresses and the strains to which the veteran has been subjected in his service, particularly while on active service, who is to say that these conditions would have developed had the veteran not enlisted at all. We feel in all these cases the veteran should receive the benefit of doubt.
Furthermore, there are cases resulting from incomplete records. The legislation as it is now administered gives the advantage to the type of person who reports to the medical officer for any ailment, however trivial. On the other hand, there are other veterans who in private life would never develop that kind of habit and have even made light of their illnesses although they were serious.
There were also cases when they did develop serious ailments but did not recognize them as such and therefore failed to report them at the proper time, and this was particularly so with regard to men on small vessels and patrol boats operating in rough waters. Small injuries occurred, but the servicemen did not think them worth bothering about and consequently there was no record of these happenings. Later on, when some complication developed from these injuries, the absence of a record handicapped them in having these disabilities attributed to service.
We regret that the government has not seen fit to embody in this bill the recommendations made by the Canadian Legion with respect to the special case of Newfoundland veterans. We regret also that the government has not seen fit to follow the established procedure and have this bill go before the committee on veterans affairs. However, we have been assured by the minister that a veterans affairs committee will be set up next

Pension Act
session and we hope the government will take the opportunity to give this legislation a thorough overhaul and bring in further legislation in accordance with the representations of the Canadian Legion and hon. members on this side of the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take very much time addressing the house because while we were on the resolution stage a number of hon. members from this group spoke and expressed their approval of the measure. The matters covered by this bill are in accordance with requests made from time to time by the committee on veterans affairs and, also, I think they go a very long way toward meeting the requests of the various veterans organizations.
When we were discussing the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs I suggested that perhaps the main weakness in the Pensions Act could be found in sections 13 and 70. Section 13 deals with disabilities of pre-enlistment origin. A great deal of time has been taken up in committees in the past in dealing with this section, and the minister has, I understand, promised that further consideration will be given to these suggestions. He has said that next session a committee on veterans affairs will be dealing with the Pensions Act and that further consideration may be given to this section at that time.
The other section is section 70-probably the most contentious section in the act,-the one about the benefit of a doubt. Here again, veterans affairs committees have spent a lot of time in the past discussing this matter, and amendments have been moved to try to improve the section, but there is still a feeling among veterans organizations that veterans today are still not getting the full benefit of the doubt. I cited a case, when we were discussing the estimates, of a veteran who had died and whose widow had been refused a pension. Since then I have received a letter from the pension commission explaining the case to me and pointing out that in the light of all the circumstances it would not be possible for them to award that widow a pension even though they gave her the full benefit of the doubt. When I raised that case I did not criticize the pension commission. I pointed out then that I believed they were going just as far as they could under the terms of section 70.
But I did suggest, and again I make the suggestion to the minister, that consideration should be given to giving the pension commission greater latitude in dealing with cases under this section. I think they should have more power and we could give them this greater power because otherwise I am sure
[Mr. Carter.!
we will continue to have complaints as we have had in the past from veterans organizations that many of the veterans who apply for help under this section are not getting the benefit of the doubt. I trust that when the committee on veterans affairs is set up next session section 70 will also be given very serious consideration.
So I will say again that we think the bill is a good bill. It goes quite a long way, and if we can make as much progress next year with regard to the other sections we will certainly have accomplished a good deal.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is one point I should like to raise at this time. I have taken this matter up with the minister and with the pensions board and I have received co-operation in every way, but it just seems to me that the way the law is at present this young woman I am going to talk about can get no help whatever. This young woman's husband was killed while going home on leave in France somewhere. This young woman has two children and can get no pension of any kind. I have had the matter explained to me. The way the law reads at present it seems nothing can be done for her, but I am going to appeal to the minister or to the government to take some action so that this woman may receive some pension.
When these young fellows went to the war they were promised anything they asked for. Here we have this chap buried in France somewhere. The wife is alive, and the only thing that keeps her from getting a pension is that her husband went on leave at six o'clock at night and was killed at eight o'clock. What difference does that make? He would never have been in France if he had not joined the air force. I do not want to dwell on this, but it does seem to me there is something wrong when we cannot do something for the women who are left. It is true that this man was not on duty when he was killed, but if he had not joined the air force he would have been driving a tractor or something else at home. But he joined the air force, and the defence of the department with regard to this pension is that he was not on duty at the time.
These fellows who enlist are going to be in the peace army and, just at the crack of the whip, in an hour's time, they can be in the war army, call it anything you like. I do hope the minister is going to do something about this case. I visited this lady and the two small children and believe me, gentlemen, it is a pitiful case and something should be done about it.
I have another case here. I went to the department to get information about it and

there is just one question I want to ask. It deals with a man who is getting a pension, and who becomes mentally sick and is confined to a mental hospital. I understand from the department that they pay for the hospitalization of that man, and have his pension accumulate. If he gets better, he gets the whole thing back. If he dies it reverts to the crown. I wonder if the minister thinks on a Saturday afternoon when the patient's relatives come to the hospital and take him this and take him that, surely if he has got a disability pension he should have the right to spend some of the money whether he is mentally sick or not. When you visit a hospital you often see the patients smoking. Who is going to give them their cigarettes? They should be allowed to buy their own. The same thing applies to the veterans allowance. If a man dies it reverts to the crown. That is accumulated over some time. These are situations which could be improved upon by amendments to the Pension Act.
I want to ask the minister one other thing. Is there anything left in the fund that was collected in connection with Hong Kong? Mr. Chairman, I am just wasting my wind here in talking because the minister is not even listening.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs

I would not criticize you for the world but I do want to know something about the Hong Kong fund. Is there any money left in it? I want to know what they are going to do with it. I know of many cases, and I am sure the minister knows of many too, involving people
Pension Act
who through war service have developed various conditions of ill health and ailments which render them unable to work. When they seek assistance they are advised that their condition has nothing to do with their enlistment and I think some consideration should be given to these matters.
Most of the other points I intended to deal with have been covered by the hon. member for Kootenay West and I support him 100 per cent in the requests he has made. I will be looking for answers to the questions we have raised when the minister rises to deal with our questions.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I might make a few remarks in connection with some of the questions that were asked. In the first place, the hon. member for Kootenay West spoke about hospitalization. I might point out that hospitalization does not come under this act. However, the hon. member mentioned some cases which came to his attention with reference to Shaugh-nessy hospital. I might say that his information is not the same as the information which we had in the department but it is our intention to investigate the criticisms that have been made by the hon. gentleman and we intend to investigate the facts. While I do not doubt the hon. member nor do I doubt the veteran who has written to him, it is often our experience that when we go over the files in these cases, we find the situation is different from what is stated in the letters which hon. members receive.
The hon. member for Kootenay West also spoke about the brief presented by the Canadian Legion; as a matter of fact, he based most of his remarks on that brief which, as hon. members know, was presented to us just a short time ago. I might point out that we have reviewed the brief with officials and representatives of the Canadian Legion and we also reviewed this bill with them. It has been nearly a month since the resolution was before the house. The bill is well known to all hon. members and also to the various veterans organizations. The Canadian Legion, I am sure, went through it with a fine tooth comb. They agreed to practically every provision in the bill with the exception of about four sections. We spent a couple of hours the other day with officials and representatives of the Legion and came to agreement with them on certain amendments to the bill.

Pension Act
With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo with reference to Newfoundland veterans, I think there is a real case there and I am very much surprised that the problem of the Newfoundland veteran has not been dealt with before this time. It should have been dealt with long ago and I am extremely surprised that this problem was not solved when the terms of confederation were discussed with Newfoundland. However, the problem which the hon. member raised with reference to the Newfoundland veteran who served with the British forces during the second world war is not different from the problem of many hundreds-I think I might say over 1,000

veterans whose domicile was in Canada before the first world war and who served in Great Britain. They receive exactly the same treatment as does the Newfoundland veteran. This is a matter which certainly should be and must be considered by a veterans committee. Any veteran who is a Canadian, whether he comes from Newfoundland or from any other part of Canada, should receive exactly the same treatment as that received by other Canadian veterans. That is my opinion and I think that would be the opinion of a veterans committee which might review the matter. I can assure the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo that it will be given every consideration.
The hon. member also mentioned the benefit of the doubt and used the words, "we feel on this side of the house". I wonder who he means by "we"? Does he mean the present opposition, the former government? I wonder why they did not feel that way over the past years? The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo was, I think, a member of the veterans affairs committee in 1952 and I did not hear him bring up this matter at that time although, as the hon. member for Acadia and other hon. members who have spoken tonight have said, this question of the benefit of the doubt has been before veterans committees on many occasions. Of course, the present opposition was then the government and were in power for some 22 years while our party has only been in power for a few months. However, this is a matter which I assure my hon. friend, will receive consideration.

speechtext: I am glad to hear that.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the minister most sincerely for the remarks he has made with respect to Newfoundland veterans, for his sympathetic attitude and for his assurance that the case of the Newfoundland veterans will be brought before a veterans affairs committee next session. The minister raised the question of why we did not bring up this matter before. There is a very simple explanation. I gave part of the explanation when I spoke on the resolution stage of the bill, but I did not want to take up the time then to go farther.
The explanation is that this kind of case had not come to our attention. The bulk of veterans cases that come to the attention of members of parliament are cases dealing with the veterans allowance, and it must be remembered, as I pointed out when

I spoke at the resolution stage, that the definition of a Newfoundland veteran in the veterans allowance act is satisfactory. We do not get very many complaints from pensioners and even those we do get are usually mixed up with the need for supplementation by veterans allowances.
The reason why we did not bring this matter up in the committee was that we did not really have any cases like these brought to our attention. We did have cases brought to our attention last year but it must be remembered that in the early part of the session the veterans affairs estimates did not come before the house and there was no opportunity to talk about the matter. In fact, it was only a short time ago that the minister brought his estimates before the house and there was an opportunity to discuss it. The minister said that there were cases similar to the Newfoundland veterans, and I think he cited British citizens who served in the Canadian forces and are now domiciled in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext: If the hon. member will pardon me, they were Canadians domiciled in Canada who went overseas voluntarily, joined the British forces and served with the British forces. There are over a thousand of them in exactly the same position as the Newfoundland men who went over and served with the Imperials. As a matter of fact, most of them were first war veterans but there are some second war.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I thank the minister most sincerely because he has just outlined the point I was going to make. He said that these were Canadian citizens domiciled in Canada who voluntarily by-passed the Canadian forces, went overseas and enlisted in the British forces. Our submission is that the Newfoundlanders are not in the same position. They did not by-pass the Canadian forces because we were not a part of Canada at that time, and so we say we are different. If there is an actual force in a person's own country and he deliberately by-passes it and enlists in the armed forces of another country that is his own business and he must take the consequences, but the Newfoundlanders did not do that. Had we been part of Canada we would have enlisted in the Canadian forces, as we did during the Korean war. The fact is that we were not a part of Canada at that time and did not by-pass the Canadian forces. We did the only thing we could do and the definition in the War Veterans' Allowance Act acknowledges that and gives us full status on the same basis as if we had served in the Canadian forces.
But in the case of the Pension Act the definition is different and is not nearly so
Pension Act
clear. The trouble is both with the wording of the definition and the interpretation which the pension commission has placed upon it. I am told that during the second world war there were some members of the Royal Canadian Air Force who, because there was a shortage of airmen in Britain, were transferred to the Royal Air Force. As I understand it, they did not volunteer. There was an emergency and Britain was short of personnel to man her planes. We had men available and they were transferred to the Royal Air Force and served in that force very much in the same way as Newfoundland servicemen served in British forces, not of their own choice but because of the exigencies of the situation and because they were required as part of the war effort in an emergency.
I should like the minister to explain this matter because I am informed that when the veterans who went from the Royal Canadian Air Force to the Royal Air Force came back to Canada some sort of deal was worked out with the British ministry of pensions whereby that body agreed to pay a flat rate and the Canadian government supplemented those pensions to the full amount. If that is wrong, I should like the minister to correct me. But if it is right, we say that the same sort of treatment should be accorded to Newfoundland veterans.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext: I assure the hon. member that he would have persuaded me if I were not persuaded before.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Before this clause is carried, I should like to bring two matters up for the consideration of the minister. I should like to ask, what more should a man do than enlist and go through a war and be a veteran in order to entitle him to treatment in any hospital in this country? What do you mean by saying any veteran should not be entitled to help whenever he needs it and wherever he needs it?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.

If the minister starts talking about being out of order we may do

Pension Act
something about it. The important fact is that this question was brought up by the hon. member for Kootenay West. The minister undertook to answer it on the first clause of the bill when we went into committee. subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
