Well, I raised the question and I have told you what I mean and what I think. I hope I never have to sit in this house and hear any more of this particular doctrine that has been advocated in this connection.
The next matter that troubles me deeply is that the minister, out of the kindness of his heart, and I appreciate it, said that the department was considering various cases with a view to bringing these cases under the act. The question comes to my mind, have we drafted this act for the veterans or are we trying to make the veterans fit the act? If we have not drafted the act for the sake of the veterans it seems to me that we have gone off the track a long way. It seems to me that a veterans' act ought to include all veterans. I just wish to bring that to the minister's attention. I will not bother him any more at the present time. I appreciate the fact that he said these cases are receiving very careful attention. I hope they receive more careful attention than they received from the Liberal party during the years and years I have sat here while they formed the government.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to make mention of this word "entitled". Reference was made by the last speaker to the fact that any veteran who signed up and went through a war was entitled to something. I do not go along with that, and for this reason. I signed up, I went through the war and I came out with an A category. It is some time since I came out, and I do not feel I am entitled to any benefits under this act. I believe the same thing would apply to anybody who has come out with an A category because it is

twelve years since that happened and I do not think we are entitled to anything under this act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext: I might say that it is the men who are big, fine, noble men like this who pave the way for trouble for their weaker brethren. There are plenty of men, I will agree, who go through a war and at the end of it think they are all right. However any soldier who enlists for a modern war and goes right through that war, no matter how well he feels at the end of his service he has had things happen to his make-up which will tell on him sooner or later. Consequently we must have our act and our policies so framed that any veteran who needs treatment will be taken care of at any time.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEPENDANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should like to say that I believe the amendments to this act are in good order. There are some things here for which the Canadian Legion has been asking for a number of years and which I feel are very necessary in order to give a measure of justice to the men who served in the two wars.
I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Lethbridge has just said. As you travel through the country and visit Legion branches you find veterans of the first war who are today feeling the effects of their service in a way that they never realized they would feel them. Men who serve in a war, even when they come out with an A category, find that when they get to be 50 or 60 years of age the war has had an effect upon them. I understand that it is difficult to legislate exactly to cover all disabilities. If one interprets the act literally word for word I can see that there is a possibility of men not receiving justice who are deserving of it.
I note that the average age of veterans in Canada who are in receipt of pensions is something like 66.8 years, that is as of March, 1957. I do believe there is need for some easing of the interpretation of the act or the medical findings of the board when an application is made. I hope that the minister will ask his officers to give consideration to cases where veterans have come through the first war and who are now feeling the effects of that war. Some of these men received a pension, some received a pension and were taken off pension, and others did not receive any pension.
I have a particular case in my own constituency in mind. I wrote the minister about it some weeks ago, and I hope he is still investigating the matter. This case concerns a man who enlisted with the Canadian army in the first war. There were many volunteers from the west. This man was

stationed in the barracks in Regina. There was a call for men to go out on harvesting leave to help with the harvesting. A great many men were called out at that time. His statement to me over a period of years has been that these men were ordered to go out on harvesting leave; the men were told they were expected to go out. His statement to me is they went on leave in that regard. He was unfortunate enough, while on leave, to have his arm badly mangled and the result was an amputation.
Apparently the officials of the department at that time-that is the Department of National Defence-thought this man deserved a pension and he received a pension of some $30 or $40 per month for the balance of the war. He continued on pension until 1919. He thought that was what was going to be paid to him. He had certainly been badly disabled, but perhaps not in active service. However, the pension was cut off and he has been denied any pension since that time. He continued all through life with his arm amputated and with that disability he carried on as best he could. The man is now retired and can no longer work. The pension he receives as a result of the work in which he was engaged is very small because he was in a more or less minor position and could not receive the same wages as an able bodied person would receive. He is now over 60 years of age. His pension is so small that he and his wife find considerable difficulty in making ends meet.
He is not a complaining man. He does his bit. He is a fine citizen. The pension commission refuses him any consideration on the ground that his service while going out on harvest leave was voluntary. He states that it was not voluntary. He only has his statement against that of the pension commission and they refuse to give any consideration to the matter. I have written to the minister and have asked him to take the case up and look into it with a view to seeing whether or not this man, for the few remaining years of his life, is not as much entitled to a pension today as he was when he first received the injury. I doubt whether the matter of whether or not he was ordered to, go on leave can be finally settled at this time. I would just ask the minister to take into consideration the fact that this man volunteered to go and was willing to serve his country. He was granted a pension during the war. Public opinion probably demanded it. When the war ended or at least shortly thereafter his pension ended. The dispute about whether or not he was sent on harvest leave has been the one thing that has barred him.

I am drawing it to the minister's attention and asking him if he will look into it and give me a reply to my letter.

The more I read this section, the more I am convinced that there is in it what I would call a loophole. In order to explain what I mean I think I shall be obliged to read the old section first. It reads as follows:
There may be appointed such number of persons as may be considered necessary, who shall be barristers or advocates of good standing at the bar of any of the provinces of Canada, to be officers of the department and to be called "pension counsel".
The amendment reads as follows:
There may be appointed such number of persons as may be considered necessary, who are or have been barristers or advocates of good standing at the bar of any province, as officers of the department to be called "pension counsel".
I fully appreciate the purpose of this amendment which, as is stated in the bill itself, is to permit the appointment of persons with training in law who have elected to make a career in the public service, whether or not they have continued to pay annual dues to their respective law societies.
I submit that when you look at the persons eligible, who are or have been barristers or solicitors in good standing at the bar of any province, you might have a barrister who has been in good standing for quite a number of years and yet has become disbarred. With the way this section reads at the present time I submit that you could have a disbarred solicitor appointed as pension counsel, advocate or officer of the department. I would submit quite respectfully to the minister that somewhere in there, possibly after the words "of any province", he should add the words "who have not been disbarred". speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, November 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Starr for the second reading of Bill No. 16, to provide for annual vacations with pay for employees in public works, undertakings and businesses.

subtopic: PROVISION OP ANNUAL VACATIONS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was on November 8 that I adjourned the debate on the second reading of this bill. The house will recall that at that period of the session we had been having considerable discussion about holidays with pay. A good deal has happened here since November 8, and possibly some hon. members may have forgotten that this was one of the topics of discussion at that time.
When I rose to speak on that occasion I drew to the attention of the house the fact that a bill somewhat similar to the one the minister is bringing in had been first introduced in this house in 1956 by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Perhaps I may also remind the house at this time that a bill similar to the one which he introduced in 1956 has been under discussion in this house under another order.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I pointed out when I was speaking for a few minutes before this debate was adjourned, the principal point of difference as far as I see it between the bill which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has brought into the house and the proposal which has been brought in on behalf of the C.C.F. group by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, is that the minister's bill requires that an employee shall be entitled to only one week's vacation with pay after a year of employment whereas the bill which we are proposing would require that employees be given at least two weeks vacation after one year's employment. That, Mr. Speaker, will be the principal point on which we differ from the minister in the bill which he has introduced. I made it clear that we were glad that at last we had a bill of this kind sponsored on the government side of the house, and that in general we had no quarrel with the minister for bringing in a bill the principle of which was to provide for annual vacations with pay.
One of the interesting things which was mentioned by my colleague the hon. member

for Skeena (Mr. Howard) when he spoke on November 8 was the fact that on July 27, 1956, ten of the members of the present government voted in favour of a bill which provided for two week's vacation with pay after one year's employment, and therefore we are somewhat at a loss to know why the present Minister of Labour has not seen fit to incorporate this provision into his bill. There is another point in the bill which we have under discussion which I think deserves some attention. When the minister introduced this bill on second reading, he pointed out on page 925 of Hansard that the provision for annual vacation does not apply if the employment is less than 30 days in duration.
Mr. Speaker, I have given this question a little thought. I have in my hand a copy of the bill providing for annual holidays with pay in British Columbia, and I think I should point out to the minister that there is no limiting factor such as he is suggesting in our British Columbia act. Section 5 of the annual holidays with pay for employees act of British Columbia provides in subsection 1, and I am quoting:
Where an employee's employment terminates before he becomes entitled to an annual holiday in accordance with section 4, the employer shall on the termination of employment pay to the employee in addition to any payment accruing to him for his service an amount equal to 4 per cent of his total wages and salary earned during the period of his employment.
As you will note, Mr. Speaker, there is no limiting period during which an employee must work for a given employer in order to be entitled to holiday pay. Theoretically, at least, if he has worked for one hour he is entitled to 4 per cent of that hour's wages when his employment is terminated, and while I am not suggesting that normal employment should be of that short duration, nevertheless this is an important question in respect to many of the tradesmen of our country. This was the experience we had when holidays with pay were first brought in by law in British Columbia; many of the tradesmen of our province, carpenters and plumbers and electricians to name only a few, were being disqualified from receiving the benefits of the legislation because of the fact that they normally did not work a full year for one employer.
Now I should like to suggest to the minister that the effect of this limitation in his bill will be to disqualify tradesmen who may be working in the employment of companies under federal jurisdiction.
As a result the tradesmen, if they happen to work in an undertaking under federal jurisdiction, are going to find themselves in

many cases entitled to less vacation pay than they would have if they confined their activities entirely to work under provincial jurisdiction. Certainly that will be the case in the province of British Columbia and I think that is a point well worth consideration because of the fact that workers in those categories normally do not engage in a continuous period of employment with any one particular employer. In their case at least there would be no validity to an argument being advanced that attachment to a certain employer for a given minimum period should be a requirement of entitlement to holiday pay.
This bill, of course, is confined to providing vacations with pay for those who are not employed by the federal government but who do come under federal labour jurisdiction. However, I think it should be considered in relation to the provisions which do apply to those who are directly employed by the federal government. According to information I received on a quick check of this matter I believe those who are classified as civil servants receive one and one-half days off for each month with pay for the purpose of vacation up to a maximum of 18 days exclusive of Sundays and holidays in one fiscal year.
Generally speaking those who are in the category of being prevailing rate employees receive one week after one year of service and two weeks after two years of service but there is one particular classification of people employed by the federal government for whom no provision for holidays is made. I refer to those who are considered to be casual employees. Those are people who may work for the government for a period of time and in this case, we will say, then work for an employer who comes under federal labour jurisdiction; as it stands those people are going to be entitled to less than the normal period of vacation with pay.
I think it might be well worth considering when we are passing a bill providing vacations with pay for employees under federal labour jurisdiction we should at the same time pick up these loose ends of employment in the government service. The minister should consider this question in relation to this bill and should be prepared before consideration of it is completed to bring in some appropriate amendment to the bill which would ensure that those who are in the direct employ of the government of Canada in any capacity are not going to be entitled to vacations with pay under conditions less favourable than those that are going to be provided in this bill.
